1. How this chapter is organised and why it decides your organic score

General Organic Chemistry (GOC) is not a list of reactions. It is the set of six or seven ideas from which every later organic mechanism is derived. A student who truly owns GOC can predict the product of a reaction that has never been seen before; a student who has only memorised reactions cannot. Every later chapter leans on a particular part of this one.

Where each GOC idea is used later in the syllabus
GOC ideaWhere it decides the answer
Hybridisation, s-characterAcidity of alkynes, bond lengths, carbanion stability, dipole moments of propene/propyne, reactivity of vinyl and aryl halides
Inductive and field effectsStrength of carboxylic acids, basicity of aliphatic amines, rate of SN1 and SN2, reactivity of carbonyl compounds toward nucleophiles
Resonance (+M, −M)Acidity of phenols, basicity of anilines and amides, orientation in electrophilic aromatic substitution, reactivity of aryl halides, enolate chemistry
HyperconjugationCarbocation and alkene stability, Saytzeff rule, orientation in addition, heats of hydrogenation
AromaticityStability and reactivity of benzene, annulenes, ions (tropylium, cyclopentadienyl), heterocycles, acidity of cyclopentadiene
Acid-base strengthWhich proton is removed, which atom is protonated, choice of base, leaving-group ability, pKₐ-based reaction feasibility
Stability of intermediatesRegiochemistry and rearrangements in nearly every mechanism
TautomerismAldol, Claisen, Michael, Fischer indole, alkylation of β-dicarbonyls, glucose mutarotation
Hydrogen bondingBoiling points, solubility, steam volatility, separation of o- and p-nitrophenol, structure of proteins and DNA
IMP The one habit that separates 90 % scorers from the rest: for every question, first write the conjugate base (or the intermediate) on paper, show where the charge or the lone pair sits, and only then compare. Almost every GOC question is the same question in disguise: where does the charge go, and how well can the molecule accommodate it?

2. Lewis structures, formal charge and the language of structures

2.1 Formal charge

Formal charge is a bookkeeping device: it assumes that every bond is shared exactly equally.

Formula Formal charge (FC) = V − N − B/2 , where V = valence electrons of the free atom, N = non-bonding (lone-pair) electrons on the atom, B = bonding electrons around the atom.
The sum of all formal charges equals the net charge of the species. The formal charge tells you where the charge is assigned, not how the electron density is really distributed: in a carboxylate ion the formal charge sits on one oxygen in each contributor, but the real charge is shared equally.
Standard bonding patterns of the common atoms in neutral molecules and the charged forms they must adopt when the pattern is changed
AtomNeutral patternPositive formNegative form
C4 bonds, no lone pair3 bonds, no lone pair (carbocation, sextet)3 bonds + 1 lone pair (carbanion)
N3 bonds + 1 lone pair4 bonds, no lone pair (ammonium, nitro N)2 bonds + 2 lone pairs (amide ion, N⁻)
O2 bonds + 2 lone pairs3 bonds + 1 lone pair (oxonium, carbonyl O–H⁺)1 bond + 3 lone pairs (alkoxide, carboxylate O⁻)
X (halogen)1 bond + 3 lone pairs2 bonds + 2 lone pairs (halonium, as in Br₂ + alkene)none (halide, 4 lone pairs)
B3 bonds, no lone pair (sextet)rare4 bonds (borate, BF₄⁻)
Exam Trap The octet rule is a guide to which contributors are important, not a law. Boron and the cations of carbon are stable enough to be intermediates with six electrons, and the elements of period 3 (S, P) in sulfones, sulfonic acids and phosphates can be written with more than eight electrons in JEE-style structures. For second-period elements (C, N, O, F) an octet is never exceeded: a structure with five bonds to carbon or nitrogen is wrong, always.
nitro group (N⁺ and O⁻ shown) nitrite ion azide ion ozone diazomethane trimethylamine N-oxide
Common structures that must carry formal charges in a correct Lewis structure
Illustration 2.1 Main

Formal charges in the nitro group

Assign formal charges to nitrogen and each oxygen in CH₃–NO₂ and explain why the structure has no octet violation although N appears to form five bonds.

  1. Nitrogen: V = 5, N = 0 lone-pair electrons, B = 8 (one single bond to C, one single bond to O⁻, one double bond to O counted as 2 bonds, total four bonds = 8 electrons). FC = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.
  2. Double-bonded oxygen: V = 6, N = 4, B = 4. FC = 6 − 4 − 2 = 0. Single-bonded oxygen: V = 6, N = 6, B = 2. FC = 6 − 6 − 1 = −1.
  3. Nitrogen has only four bonds (C–N, N–O, N=O counts as two): 4 bonds = 8 electrons, a full octet. Writing N=O as a double bond to both oxygens (five bonds to N) would put ten electrons on a second-period atom and is not allowed. The charge-separated structure is the correct Lewis picture and the two N–O bonds are equal in the real molecule (resonance).
Illustration 2.2 Main

Formal charges in the azide ion

The azide ion N₃⁻ has 16 valence electrons. Write two valid Lewis structures, assign formal charges, and state which atom is positive in every contributor.

  1. Structure I, symmetric: [:N̤=N=N:] with each terminal nitrogen carrying two lone pairs and a double bond to the central nitrogen. Terminal N: FC = 5 − 4 − 2 = −1. Central N (two double bonds, no lone pair): FC = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. Sum = −1 + 1 − 1 = −1 ✓.
  2. Structure II: one terminal N is joined to the centre by a triple bond and carries one lone pair, the other terminal N is joined by a single bond and carries three lone pairs. Triple-bonded N: FC = 5 − 2 − 3 = 0. Central N: FC = 5 − 0 − 4 = +1. Single-bonded N: FC = 5 − 6 − 1 = −2. Sum = 0 + 1 − 2 = −1 ✓.
  3. The central nitrogen is +1 in every contributor (it has four bonds and no lone pair). Structure I, with the negative charge spread over two atoms and no −2 charge, is the major contributor, so the two N–N bonds are equal (about 116 pm) and intermediate between N=N and N≡N.

2.2 Writing structures: condensed, bond-line and what hides in them

In a bond-line formula every vertex and every end of a line is a carbon, hydrogens on carbon are not drawn, and every carbon is assumed to have enough hydrogens to make four bonds. Heteroatoms and their hydrogens are always drawn. Practise converting freely between the three forms; the questions of the following sections assume you can count hydrogens and identify α, β positions instantly.

CH₃CH₂CH(CH₃)COOH cyclohexanone acetylsalicylic acid nicotine caffeine
Bond-line structures: count carbons at vertices, hydrogens implied

2.3 Degree of unsaturation (DBE) and its uses

Formula DBE = C + 1 + (N − H − X)/2 (O and S do not change the count; N counts +½ each, H and halogens −½ each).
Each ring and each π-bond counts 1, each triple bond counts 2. For benzene (C₆H₆): 6 + 1 − 3 = 4 (one ring + three π bonds). DBE is the quickest check that a formula you have drawn is consistent with its molecular formula, and it limits the number of rings/π-bonds an unknown can contain.
Illustration 2.3 Main

DBE of nicotine and caffeine

Find the degree of unsaturation of nicotine (C₁₀H₁₄N₂) and caffeine (C₈H₁₀N₄O₂).

  1. Nicotine: DBE = 10 + 1 + (2 − 14)/2 = 11 − 6 = 5 (pyridine ring: 1 ring + 3 C=C/C=N = 4; pyrrolidine ring: 1; total 5 ✓).
  2. Caffeine: DBE = 8 + 1 + (4 − 10)/2 = 9 − 3 = 6 (two rings, two C=O, two C=C/C=N in the ring system = 6 ✓).

2.4 Types of carbon and hydrogen

A carbon is primary (1°), secondary (2°), tertiary (3°) or quaternary (4°) according to the number of other carbons it is bonded to (1, 2, 3, 4). Hydrogens are named for the carbon that carries them. Special names: allylic (on a carbon next to C=C), vinylic (on a C=C carbon), benzylic (on a carbon next to a benzene ring), α-hydrogen (on a carbon next to a carbonyl group or other functional group; in carbocation chemistry, on the carbon next to the cationic centre). Counting types of hydrogen is the first step of every hyperconjugation and radical-stability question.

Illustration 2.4 Main

Counting types of carbon

In 2,2,4-trimethylpentane (isooctane) find the number of primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary carbons and the number of primary hydrogens.

  1. Skeleton: (CH₃)₃C–CH₂–CH(CH₃)–CH₃. Carbons: the three CH₃ on C-2 and the two CH₃ on C-4 are all bonded to one carbon → 5 primary carbons. CH₂ is bonded to two carbons → 1 secondary. The CH is bonded to three carbons → 1 tertiary. C-2 is bonded to four carbons → 1 quaternary.
  2. Primary hydrogens are those on primary carbons: 5 × 3 = 15.
2,2,4-trimethylpentane

3. Hybridisation

3.1 The idea and the three hybrid sets of carbon

A free carbon atom has the configuration 1s²2s²2p². To make four equivalent bonds the 2s orbital is mixed with the 2p orbitals: the number of hybrid orbitals produced equals the number of atomic orbitals mixed. The three types of hybridisation of carbon are summarised below.

Hybridisation of carbon at a glance
HybridisationOrbitals mixeds-characterp-characterGeometryBond angleUnhybridised p orbitalsExample
sp³s + 3p25 %75 %tetrahedral109.5°noneCH₄, C₂H₆
sp²s + 2p33.3 %66.7 %trigonal planar120°one (forms one π bond)C₂H₄, C₆H₆, C=O carbon
sps + p50 %50 %linear180°two (form two π bonds)C₂H₂, CO₂, R–C≡N
IMP Counting rule for carbon. Count the number of σ-bonded neighbours plus lone pairs (the *steric number*): 4 → sp³, 3 → sp², 2 → sp. For carbon in stable molecules this is the same as: only single bonds → sp³; one double bond → sp²; one triple bond or two double bonds → sp.
For any atom: steric number = (number of σ-bonds) + (number of lone pairs); 4 → sp³, 3 → sp², 2 → sp, and the 'extra' bonds beyond the first to the same neighbour are π-bonds made from unhybridised p orbitals. A π-bond is never counted in the steric number.
ethane (sp³,sp³) ethene (sp²,sp²) ethyne (sp,sp) allene (sp², sp, sp²) ketene (sp², sp) carbon dioxide (sp) acetonitrile (sp³, sp, N sp) 1,3-butadiene (all sp²)
Hybridisation of the carbons in standard molecules
Illustration 3.1 Main

Hybridisation of carbons in a chain

Give the hybridisation of each carbon in CH₃–CH=CH–C≡CH.

  1. C-1 (CH₃): four σ-bonds → sp³. C-2 and C-3 (CH=CH): three σ-neighbours each → sp². C-4 and C-5 (C≡CH): two σ-neighbours each → sp.
  2. So there is one sp³, two sp² and two sp carbons.
pent-3-en-1-yne

3.2 Hybridisation of nitrogen, oxygen and the heteroatoms

Lone pairs occupy hybrid orbitals, so they count in the steric number. The one complication is conjugation: a lone pair that is delocalised into an adjacent π-system must sit in a p orbital, and an atom whose lone pair is in a p orbital is classified sp² (it becomes planar). This is why the nitrogen of an amide is sp² but the nitrogen of an amine is sp³.

Hybridisation of N and O in common situations (conjugation rule applied)
SpeciesAtomSteric number reasoningHybridisation
NH₃, R₃NN3 σ + 1 lone pair = 4sp³
R₂C=NR (imine), pyridineN2 σ + 1 lone pair (in the ring plane) = 3sp²
R–C≡NN1 σ + 1 lone pair = 2sp
Amide RCONH₂Nlone pair delocalised into C=O → p orbitalsp² (planar)
PyrroleNlone pair is part of the aromatic sextet → p orbitalsp²
AnilineNlone pair partly delocalised into the ring (slightly pyramidal)between sp³ and sp² (treated as sp² when asked about delocalisation)
PyridineNlone pair in sp² orbital in the ring plane (not part of the π-sextet)sp²
H₂O, ROH, RORO2 σ + 2 lone pairs = 4sp³
C=OO1 σ + 2 lone pairs = 3sp²
FuranOone lone pair in the sextet (p), the other in the planesp²
Ester R–C(=O)–O–R′alkoxy Olone pair delocalised into C=Osp²

Nitrogen and oxygen in different environments
Exam Trap Pyrrole and pyridine both contain an sp² nitrogen but behave completely differently: in pyridine the lone pair is in the plane, orthogonal to the π cloud and free to take a proton (basic); in pyrrole the lone pair is part of the six-electron π cloud and cannot be protonated without destroying aromaticity (non-basic). This is the single most tested nitrogen distinction.
Illustration 3.2 Adv

Hybridisation in a drug molecule

In paracetamol (4-hydroxyacetanilide) state the hybridisation of every non-hydrogen atom and the numbers of σ and π bonds.

  1. Methyl C: sp³. Carbonyl C and carbonyl O: sp². Amide N: sp² (its lone pair is delocalised into C=O). The six ring carbons: sp². Phenolic O: its lone pair overlaps with the ring π system, so it is sp² in the resonance sense (a question that asks for 'steric-number hybridisation' would call it sp³; read the wording).
  2. σ-bonds: every bond contributes one σ. With hydrogens counted explicitly the molecule has 20 bonds when each double bond is counted once: 6 ring C–C, 5 chain bonds (CH₃–C, C–O, C–N, N–C(ring), C(ring)–O), 9 X–H bonds (3 C–H of CH₃, 4 aromatic C–H, 1 N–H, 1 O–H). Total σ = 6 + 5 + 9 = 20.
  3. π-bonds: 3 in the ring (Kekulé form) + 1 in C=O = 4. Check by DBE: C₈H₉NO₂ gives 8 + 1 + (1 − 9)/2 = 5 = one ring + 4 π-bonds ✓.
paracetamol

3.3 s-character: the single most useful number

The 2s orbital is lower in energy and held closer to the nucleus than the 2p orbitals. Therefore the greater the s-character of a hybrid orbital, the more tightly its electrons are held, the shorter and stronger the bond it forms, and the more electronegative that carbon appears. All four properties of Table 3.3 follow from this one statement.

Properties that change smoothly with s-character
Propertysp³ (25 % s)sp² (33 % s)sp (50 % s)
Apparent electronegativity of C≈ 2.5≈ 2.75≈ 3.3
C–H bond length (pm)109 (ethane)108 (ethene)106 (ethyne)
C–H bond dissociation enthalpy (kJ mol⁻¹)423 (ethane)465 (ethene)558 (ethyne)
C–C single bond to a methyl group (pm)154 (ethane)150 (propene)146 (propyne)
pKₐ of the C–H≈ 50≈ 44≈ 25
Dipole moment of CH₃–X, X = propane/propene/propyne0.08 D0.36 D0.78 D
Stability of the carbanionlowestmiddlehighest
IMP Increasing s-character ⟹ shorter bond, stronger bond, higher electronegativity of that carbon, higher acidity of the attached H, lower stability of the corresponding carbocation, higher stability of the carbanion, larger bond angle.
Illustration 3.3 Main

Rank by C–H bond length

Arrange in decreasing C–H bond length: ethane, ethene, ethyne, benzene.

  1. s-character: ethane sp³ (25 %), ethene and benzene sp² (33 %), ethyne sp (50 %). A greater s-character shortens the bond.
  2. Ethane (109 pm) > ethene (108.5 pm) ≈ benzene (108 pm) > ethyne (106 pm).
  3. Ethane > ethene ≈ benzene > ethyne. In JEE style the two sp² compounds are treated as equal.
Illustration 3.4 Adv

Dipole moment from hybridisation

Propane is almost non-polar (0.08 D) whereas propene has μ = 0.36 D and propyne μ = 0.78 D. Give the direction of the dipole in propene and propyne and explain why propyne is more polar.

  1. The CH₃ group is attached to a carbon that is sp² (33 % s) in propene and sp (50 % s) in propyne. A carbon with more s-character holds electrons more tightly, so it behaves as the more electronegative end of the C–C bond. The dipole therefore points from CH₃ (δ+) toward the unsaturated carbon (δ−).
  2. The difference in s-character between the two carbons of the σ-bond is larger in propyne (50 % vs 25 %) than in propene (33 % vs 25 %), so μ(propyne) > μ(propene). Hyperconjugation (σ C–H → π*) pushes density the same way and adds to the effect.
propene propyne
μ = 0.36 D and 0.78 D

Illustration 3.5 Adv

Allene geometry and chirality

Explain why the two CH₂ planes of allene lie at 90° and why penta-2,3-diene CH₃CH=C=CHCH₃ can exist as a pair of enantiomers.

  1. The central carbon is sp-hybridised. Its two unhybridised p orbitals are perpendicular to each other; one overlaps with the p orbital on the left carbon and the other with the p orbital on the right carbon. The two π bonds are therefore in perpendicular planes.
  2. The substituents on each terminal carbon lie in the plane perpendicular to the π bond of that carbon, so the two CH₂ (or CHCH₃) planes are at 90° to each other.
  3. In CH₃CH=C=CHCH₃ each terminal carbon carries two different groups (H and CH₃). The molecule has no plane of symmetry and no centre of symmetry, so it has a chiral axis and exists as two non-superimposable mirror images. If either terminal carbon carries two identical groups, a mirror plane exists and the allene is achiral.
allene penta-2,3-diene
Illustration 3.6 Integer

σ and π count

Find the total number of σ and π bonds in tetracyanoethene (NC)₂C=C(CN)₂ and report σ + π.

  1. Bonds: one C=C (1σ + 1π), four C–C(N) single bonds (4σ), four C≡N triple bonds (4σ + 8π).
  2. σ = 1 + 4 + 4 = 9; π = 1 + 8 = 9. σ + π = 18.
tetracyanoethene

4. Bond lengths, bond strengths and bond angles

4.1 What controls bond length

Bond length is the distance between the two nuclei at the minimum of the potential-energy curve. Five factors decide it, and almost every 'compare the bond lengths' question needs only the first three.

  • Bond order: triple < double < single (more shared electrons pull the nuclei closer).
  • s-character of the hybrid orbitals used: more s ⟹ shorter (Section 3.3).
  • Atomic size: a bond to a bigger atom is longer (C–F < C–Cl < C–Br < C–I).
  • Resonance averages the bond orders of the bonds involved: a single bond that gains partial double-bond character is shortened; a double bond that loses some π-character is lengthened.
  • Steric and electrostatic strain can lengthen a bond, especially in crowded molecules.

Exam Trap Bond length and bond strength do not always move together. Normally a shorter bond is a stronger bond (C≡C > C=C > C–C in strength). But for the halogens, C–F is the shortest C–X bond and the strongest, yet F–F (158 kJ mol⁻¹) is the weakest of the X–X bonds because of lone-pair repulsion; and the order of X–X bond enthalpy is Cl–Cl (243) > Br–Br (193) > F–F (158) > I–I (151). Check the pair of atoms before you generalise.
Illustration 4.1 Main

Ranking bond lengths

Arrange the following in increasing order of C–C bond length: ethane, benzene, ethene, ethyne.

  1. Bond order: ethyne (3) < ethene (2) < benzene (1.5) < ethane (1).
  2. Increasing length: ethyne (120 pm) < ethene (134 pm) < benzene (139 pm) < ethane (154 pm).
Illustration 4.2 Adv

Bond lengths in resonance systems

Predict which is longer in each pair and give the reason: (a) C–Cl in CH₂=CH–Cl or CH₃CH₂Cl; (b) C–O in CH₃COO⁻ or in CH₃COOH (the single-bonded C–O); (c) C–N in CH₃NH₂ or in CH₃CONH₂.

  1. (a) Chloroethane is longer. In vinyl chloride the carbon is sp² (more s-character than sp³) and a lone pair of Cl is delocalised into the C=C (+M of Cl), giving the C–Cl bond some double-bond character. Both effects shorten the bond: 172 pm vs 177 pm.
  2. (b) The C–OH bond of acetic acid is longer (about 136 pm) than either C–O bond of the acetate ion (about 126 pm, bond order 1.5). The acid has one pure C=O (122 pm) and one pure C–OH; in the ion the two bonds are equalised.
  3. (c) The C–N of methylamine is longer (147 pm) because the lone pair of nitrogen in the amide is delocalised into the carbonyl and the amide C–N has double-bond character (133 pm).
vinyl chloride vs chloroethane carboxylate vs acetic acid methylamine vs acetamide

4.2 Bond angles in molecules with lone pairs

Valence-shell electron-pair repulsion (VSEPR) gives the first-order angle, and the following corrections account for the real values.

  • Repulsion order: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair. Each lone pair squeezes the bond angle: CH₄ 109.5°, NH₃ 107°, H₂O 104.5°.
  • Electronegative substituents pull the bonding electrons away from the central atom, reducing bond-pair–bond-pair repulsion, so the angle closes: NH₃ 107° > NF₃ 102°; H₂O 104.5° > OF₂ 103°.
  • Large substituents open the angle by steric repulsion: H₂O 104.5° < (CH₃)₂O 112° and Cl₂O 111°; NH₃ 107° < (CH₃)₃N 111°.
  • Central atoms from period 3 and below use almost pure p orbitals for bonding and keep the lone pair in an s-rich orbital (the electropositive/large central atom does not hybridise), giving angles near 90°: H₂O 104.5° ≫ H₂S 92°; NH₃ 107° ≫ PH₃ 93.5° ≫ AsH₃ 92°.
  • Delocalisation of the lone pair into an adjacent π-system or empty d orbital flattens the centre: N(SiH₃)₃ is planar (angle 120°), whereas N(CH₃)₃ is pyramidal; the Si–O–Si angle in disiloxanes (about 144°) is far wider than the C–O–C angle (112°).

IMP Bent's rule. A more electronegative substituent is placed in the hybrid orbital with more p-character, and the lone pair or an electropositive substituent takes the orbital with more s-character. Corollaries: the bond angle between two highly electronegative substituents is smaller than 109.5° (F–C–F in CH₂F₂ ≈ 108°); the H–C–H angle in CH₂F₂ is larger; the lone pair of NH₃ lies in an s-rich orbital; a C–H bond on a carbon that carries an electronegative group has more s-character and is stronger.
Illustration 4.3 Main

Ranking bond angles

Arrange in decreasing bond angle: H₂O, NH₃, H₂S, CH₄, PH₃.

  1. Angles: CH₄ (109.5°, no lone pair) > NH₃ (107°) > H₂O (104.5°) among the second-row hydrides. Third-row hydrides are close to 90°: PH₃ 93.5° and H₂S 92°.
  2. CH₄ > NH₃ > H₂O > PH₃ > H₂S.
Illustration 4.4 Adv

Why is N(SiH₃)₃ planar and N(CH₃)₃ pyramidal?

Give two consequences of the difference for basicity and for the Si–O–Si angle.

  1. In trimethylamine the nitrogen lone pair has nowhere to go: N is sp³, the lone pair is localised and available, the molecule is pyramidal (C–N–C ≈ 111°).
  2. In trisilylamine silicon has empty 3d orbitals (and low-lying σ* Si–H orbitals) that overlap with the lone pair on N: p(N) → d(Si) back-bonding. The lone pair is delocalised, N becomes sp² and planar, and the compound is only a very weak Lewis base (it does not even form a stable adduct with BF₃ whereas trimethylamine does).
  3. The same effect is why the Si–O–Si angle in siloxanes (about 144°) is much wider than the C–O–C angle in ethers (112°): the oxygen lone pairs are partly delocalised into silicon.
trimethylamine trisilylamine disiloxane

5. Dipole moment

5.1 Definition and units

When two atoms of different electronegativity share a bonding pair, the pair is displaced toward the more electronegative atom, creating partial charges +δ and −δ separated by a distance d. The dipole moment is μ = q × d. It is a vector, drawn here from the positive end to the negative end (the physics convention) with a cross at the positive end: +→. (Some texts draw the arrow from negative to positive; JEE solutions use the symbol with the head at the negative end.) The unit is the debye: 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m = 10⁻¹⁸ esu cm.

Formula μ = q × d ; q ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C and d ≈ 10⁻¹⁰ m give μ ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻²⁹ C m ≈ 4.8 D
Formula % ionic character = (μ observed / μ calculated for full charges e × d) × 100
Percent ionic character from the dipole moment (e × d with the real bond length)

Illustration 5.1 Main

% ionic character of HCl

Calculate the percentage ionic character of HCl: μ = 1.08 D, bond length = 127.4 pm. (e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, 1 D = 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ C m)

  1. μ(full charges) = e × d = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C × 127.4 × 10⁻¹² m = 2.041 × 10⁻²⁹ C m = 2.041 × 10⁻²⁹ / 3.336 × 10⁻³⁰ D = 6.12 D.
  2. % ionic = 1.08 / 6.12 × 100 = 17.6 % (about 18 %).

5.2 The vector method

The dipole moment of a molecule is the vector sum of all the bond moments (and of the lone-pair contributions, which point from the nucleus outward along the lone-pair axis). The vector sum of two moments of magnitudes μ₁ and μ₂ with the angle θ between the two vectors, both drawn outward from a common origin, is

Formula μ² = μ₁² + μ₂² + 2 μ₁ μ₂ cos θ ; for equal moments μ₁ = μ₂ = μ : resultant = 2 μ cos(θ/2)
<svg viewBox="0 0 260 190" width="260" height="190" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="color:#1b2130"><defs><marker id="ah" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z" fill="#2563eb"/></marker><marker id="ar" markerWidth="8" markerHeight="8" refX="7" refY="4" orient="auto"><path d="M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 z" fill="#dc2626"/></marker></defs><line x1="130" y1="165" x2="111.3" y2="132.6" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="130" y1="165" x2="148.7" y2="132.6" stroke="#2563eb" stroke-width="2.4" marker-end="url(#ah)"/><line x1="130" y1="165" x2="130.0" y2="100.2" stroke="#dc2626" stroke-width="2.8" stroke-dasharray="6 3" marker-end="url(#ar)"/><path d="M144.0 140.8 A28 28 0 0 1 116.0 140.8" fill="none" stroke="#586275" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="130" y="131" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle" style="fill:#586275">60°</text><text x="107.3" y="132.6" font-size="12" style="fill:#2563eb" font-weight="700" text-anchor="end">μ₁ = 1.7 D</text><text x="152.7" y="132.6" font-size="12" style="fill:#2563eb" font-weight="700">μ₂ = 1.7 D</text><text x="180" y="132" font-size="12" style="fill:#dc2626" font-weight="700" text-anchor="middle">resultant = 2.94 D</text></svg>
  • θ = 0° (vectors parallel): resultant = μ₁ + μ₂ — maximum.
  • θ = 180° (vectors opposite): resultant = |μ₁ − μ₂|; zero if equal.
  • θ = 90°: resultant = √(μ₁² + μ₂²).

Two quick rules follow: a molecule whose bond moments cancel by symmetry (CO₂, CS₂, BF₃, CCl₄, SF₆, trans-1,2-dichloroethene, p-dichlorobenzene, benzene, ethene, ethane in the staggered form…) has μ = 0; and a molecule with a lone pair or a missing substituent is almost always polar.

water (104.5°, 1.85 D) ammonia (1.47 D) carbon dioxide (0 D) boron trifluoride (0 D) carbon tetrachloride (0 D) chloroform (1.0 D)
Symmetric molecules have μ = 0
Illustration 5.2 Main

Bond moment of O–H from the molecular dipole

Water has μ = 1.85 D and the H–O–H angle is 104.5°. Find the O–H bond moment (ignore lone-pair contribution).

  1. The two O–H vectors have equal magnitude m and make an angle of 104.5° with each other. The resultant is 2 m cos(104.5°/2) = 2 m cos 52.25°.
  2. cos 52.25° = 0.6122, so 1.85 = 2 m × 0.6122 ⟹ m = 1.51 D.
  3. Because lone pairs also contribute along the same direction as the vector sum, the real O–H bond moment is smaller (about 1.5 D is the textbook result when lone pairs are ignored).
Illustration 5.3 Main

Two dipoles at an angle

Two bond moments of 1.5 D and 2.0 D make an angle of 60°. What is the resultant?

  1. μ² = 1.5² + 2.0² + 2 × 1.5 × 2.0 × cos 60° = 2.25 + 4.00 + 3.00 = 9.25.
  2. μ = √9.25 = 3.04 D.

5.3 Disubstituted benzenes

For a monosubstituted benzene C₆H₅X the group moment points along the C–X axis. In disubstituted benzenes the two axes are separated by 60° (ortho), 120° (meta) and 180° (para), so the ortho isomer has the largest resultant (smallest angle) and the para isomer the smallest. When the two groups are identical:

Dipole moments of the three nitrochlorobenzenes

Using μ(C₆H₅NO₂) = 4.0 D and μ(C₆H₅Cl) = 1.6 D (both directed ring → substituent), calculate the dipole moments of the ortho, meta and para isomers of chloronitrobenzene by the vector method.

  1. Ortho (θ = 60°): μ² = 4.0² + 1.6² + 2(4.0)(1.6) cos 60° = 16 + 2.56 + 6.4 = 24.96 ⟹ μ = 5.0 D.

  4. Order ortho > meta > para. (Measured: 4.3, 3.4, 2.5 D, so the pattern is confirmed.)

Order of dipole moments

A rotating dipole

Suppose the anti conformer of 1,2-dichloroethane has μ = 0 and the gauche conformer (dihedral 60°) has μ = 2.6 D, and the measured moment of the equilibrium mixture at 25 °C is 1.1 D. Estimate the total mole fraction of gauche conformer using μ²(observed) = x μ²(gauche) + (1 − x) μ²(anti).

  1. The measured value is a weighted average of squares of the moments (the dipole-moment-squared averaging that applies to a rapidly interconverting mixture). μ²(observed) = 1.21; μ²(gauche) = 6.76; μ²(anti) = 0.

5.5 Applications of the dipole moment

  • Shape of molecules: μ = 0 for CO₂ shows it is linear; μ ≠ 0 for SO₂ and H₂O shows they are bent; NH₃ μ = 1.47 D shows pyramidal rather than planar.
  • Separating geometric isomers: the cis isomer has the larger dipole moment than the trans in 1,2-disubstituted ethenes; the more polar isomer has higher boiling point, but the less polar (more symmetrical) trans isomer usually has the higher melting point.
  • Solubility and miscibility: like dissolves like; polar solutes dissolve in polar solvents; non-polar solutes in non-polar solvents.
  • Position of substituents in aromatic rings: o-, m-, p- isomers distinguished by μ (para lowest).
  • Percent ionic character of a polar covalent bond.
  • Intermolecular forces: dipole–dipole attraction raises boiling points (e.g. propanone 56 °C vs butane −0.5 °C, similar masses).
IMP Summary sheet — Dipole moment. (1) μ = q × d, a vector from δ+ to δ−. (2) Resultant of two vectors: √(μ₁² + μ₂² + 2μ₁μ₂ cos θ). (3) Lone pairs contribute. (4) Symmetry gives zero. (5) o > m > p for identical polar groups. (6) Donor (NH₂, CH₃) and acceptor (NO₂) at para: moments add. (7) CH₃F, CH₃Cl order is a charge × length effect, not just electronegativity. (8) NH₃ > NF₃ because the lone-pair moment opposes the N–F moments.

6. The inductive effect (I effect)

6.1 Definition and origin

Whenever a σ-bond joins two atoms of different electronegativity, the bonding pair is displaced toward the more electronegative atom. This displacement does not stop at that bond: it polarises the next σ-bond, which polarises the next, and so on. This permanent polarisation transmitted through a chain of σ-bonds is the inductive effect.

  • −I (electron-withdrawing) group: pulls σ-electrons toward itself — it is more electronegative than hydrogen (the reference), e.g. –NO₂, –CN, –F, –Cl, –COOH, –OH.
  • +I (electron-releasing) group: pushes σ-electrons away from itself — it is less electronegative than hydrogen (as judged in the conventional series), e.g. –CH₃, –C₂H₅, –C(CH₃)₃, –O⁻, –COO⁻.

The effect is written with arrows on the bonds: C → C → C → Cl (the arrow head toward the electronegative end), or with a small δ⁺ that diminishes along the chain.

IMP Four properties of the I effect. (1) It is permanent — present in the ground state. (2) It operates through σ-bonds only, and each σ-bond passes on roughly half or less of the effect: it is felt strongly at the first carbon, about one half or less at the second, and is negligible beyond the third (or fourth) carbon. (3) It never reverses the sign of the polarity: the atom nearest the group is the most affected. (4) It does not involve displacement of electrons into π-orbitals or lone pairs; that is resonance.
The decay with distance is clearly seen in the pKₐ of chlorobutanoic acids (Cl placed progressively farther from the COOH):

Exam Trap Three common slips. (a) Halogens: the −I order follows electronegativity, F > Cl > Br > I, so fluoroacetic acid is the strongest of the four halogen-substituted acetic acids (pKₐ 2.6 vs 2.9, 2.9 and 3.2). (b) Hybridisation of the group's carbon: the group's −I increases with the s-character of the carbon attached: –C≡CH (sp) > –CH=CH₂ (sp²) > –CH₂CH₃ (sp³). (c) Alkyl groups are weak donors; the order t-Bu > i-Pr > Et > Me is a +I (and polarisability) order used in JEE for gas-phase and carbocation questions. In some solution phenomena the order of electron release appears reversed (the Baker–Nathan order, explained by solvation of the groups rather than by hyperconjugation alone) — do not use this unless the question says so.

Strength of chloroacetic acids

Arrange in decreasing acid strength: CH₃COOH, ClCH₂COOH, Cl₂CHCOOH, Cl₃CCOOH, CH₃CH₂COOH.

Acids with different groups on the α-carbon

  2. O₂NCH₂COOH (1.68) > NCCH₂COOH (2.47) > FCH₂COOH (2.59) > HOCH₂COOH (3.83) > C₆H₅CH₂COOH (4.31) > CH₃COOH (4.76).
Illustration 6.4 Adv

Why formic acid is stronger than acetic acid

Formic acid pKₐ 3.75, acetic acid 4.76. Explain, and say why hydrogen bonding is not the explanation.

  1. In acetate the +I group CH₃ pushes electrons toward the carboxylate carbon and oxygens, increasing the electron density on the anion and destabilising it relative to formate, in which there is only H (reference). A less stable conjugate base means a weaker acid.
  2. Hydrogen bonding is not responsible: it is a physical (intermolecular) interaction and both acids dimerise in the same way. The difference is electronic (inductive).

6.3 Where the inductive effect matters

  • Acid strength: −I groups stabilise the conjugate base. In carboxylic acids, X–CH₂COOH is stronger than CH₃COOH if X is −I and weaker if X is +I.
  • Base strength: +I groups on N raise the electron density on nitrogen and increase basicity (ammonia < methylamine in the gas phase); −I groups lower it (2,2,2-trifluoroethylamine pKₐ(H) 5.7 against ethylamine 10.7).
  • Carbocations are stabilised by +I groups (tertiary > secondary > primary); carbanions by −I groups.
  • Reactivity of carbonyl compounds toward nucleophiles: the carbon of C=O is more δ⁺ when attached to −I groups: Cl₃CCHO (chloral, forms a stable hydrate) > HCHO > CH₃CHO > CH₃COCH₃.
  • Acid derivatives: RCOCl > (RCO)₂O > RCOOR′ > RCONH₂ in reactivity toward nucleophiles (the leaving group and the electron demand at C=O).
  • Polarity and dipole direction (propene, toluene, alkyl halides).
Illustration 6.5 Adv

Basicity and the inductive effect

Arrange in increasing basicity (aqueous): CF₃CH₂NH₂, CH₃CH₂NH₂, HOCH₂CH₂NH₂, NH₃. Give reasons.

  1. The conjugate-acid pKₐ values (pKₐH) are: CF₃CH₂NH₃⁺ 5.7; NH₄⁺ 9.25; HOCH₂CH₂NH₃⁺ 9.5; CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ 10.7.
  2. The three F atoms withdraw electron density strongly from N (the lone pair is less available); an OH group two carbons away withdraws only slightly; ethyl donates.
  3. CF₃CH₂NH₂ < NH₃ < HOCH₂CH₂NH₂ < CH₃CH₂NH₂.
2,2,2-trifluoroethylamine 2-aminoethanol ethylamine ammonia

6.4 Field effect: the through-space relative

The field effect is the electrostatic influence of a polar substituent on a reaction centre transmitted through space (or through the solvent) rather than through bonds. It is hard to separate from the inductive effect in flexible molecules, because both fall off with distance and both vary with the polarity of the group. It becomes visible in rigid molecules in which the through-bond path is long but the through-space distance is short.

oxalic malonic succinic glutaric adipic
pKₐ₁ = 1.25, 2.85, 4.21, 4.34, 4.41

The pKₐ₁ of the α,ω-dicarboxylic acids rise toward 4.8 (the value for an alkanoic acid) as the second COOH moves away: 1.25 (oxalic), 2.85 (malonic), 4.21 (succinic), 4.34 (glutaric), 4.41 (adipic). The second group both withdraws electrons through the bonds and exerts a field effect on the departing proton. The pKₐ₂ values fall in the same series for the opposite reason: 4.27, 5.70, 5.64, 5.41, 5.41 — the first-formed carboxylate makes the removal of the second proton harder, and the closer it is, the harder.

Illustration 6.6 Adv

Statement test

State whether true or false: (a) The inductive effect operates through π-bonds. (b) The inductive effect is temporary. (c) +I effect of alkyl groups is greater for –CH₃ than for –C(CH₃)₃. (d) −I effect of –C≡CH is greater than that of –CH=CH₂.

  1. (a) False — it operates through σ-bonds (the π-bond version is the mesomeric or electromeric effect).
  2. (b) False — the inductive effect is permanent; the electromeric effect is temporary.
  3. (c) False — the +I order is t-Bu > i-Pr > Et > Me; the t-butyl group is the stronger donor.
  4. (d) True — the carbon of the ethynyl group is sp (50 % s), vinyl is sp² (33 % s), so ethynyl is more electron-withdrawing.

7. The electromeric effect (E effect)

7.1 Definition

The electromeric effect is the complete and temporary transfer of a shared π-electron pair to one of the two atoms joined by a multiple bond, under the influence of an attacking reagent. It appears at the moment the reagent approaches and disappears when the reagent is removed. In effect it is the very first step of every polar addition to a double bond, drawn as a curved arrow.

  • +E effect: the π-electrons are transferred toward the atom to which the attacking reagent attaches — the attacking species is an electrophile (H⁺, Br⁺, NO₂⁺, ...) and a bond to the reagent is formed at that atom.
  • −E effect: the π-electrons are transferred away from the atom to which the reagent attaches — the attacking species is a nucleophile (CN⁻, OH⁻, R⁻, ...), the π-pair moves to the other atom.
+ +E⟶
+E: π electrons move to the carbon bonded to H⁺ (propene and H⁺ give the 2° cation)
+ −E⟶
−E: π pair of C=O moves to oxygen as CN⁻ bonds to carbon (cyanohydrin formation)
IMP Electromeric vs mesomeric vs inductive. Inductive: σ-bonds, permanent, partial. Mesomeric: π-bond or lone pair in conjugation, permanent, partial (shown by resonance structures). Electromeric: single multiple bond, temporary, complete transfer, needs a reagent. When both an electromeric effect and a mesomeric effect are possible, the mesomeric effect is the ground-state polarisation and the electromeric effect the extra push by the reagent; they usually act in the same direction.
Three effects compared
FeatureInductiveMesomeric (resonance)Electromeric
Mediumσ-bondπ-bond / lone pair in conjugationan isolated π-bond
Permanencepermanentpermanenttemporary (on reagent)
Extent of electron shiftpartial (δ)partial (hybrid)complete transfer
Needs reagent?nonoyes

Illustration 7.1 Main

Direction of the electromeric effect

In each case say whether the electromeric effect is +E or −E: (a) CH₂=CH₂ attacked by H⁺ (b) CH₃CHO attacked by CN⁻ (c) CH₃CH=CH₂ attacked by Br⁺ (d) acetone attacked by H⁺ on oxygen.

  1. (a) The reagent is an electrophile and the π-pair moves toward the carbon that bonds the electrophile: +E.
  2. (b) The nucleophile CN⁻ attacks carbon, the π-pair moves to oxygen, away from the attacked carbon: −E.
  3. (c) Br⁺ electrophile: +E (the π electrons move toward the carbon that bonds Br⁺; the other carbon carries the positive charge, preferably C-2).
  4. (d) An electrophile (H⁺) attaches to O and the π electrons move toward O: +E, making the carbonyl carbon strongly δ⁺ (the first step of acid-catalysed addition).
Illustration 7.2 Adv

Markovnikov addition explained with E and I effects

Use the +I (hyperconjugative) effect of CH₃ and the +E effect to explain why HBr adds to propene to give 2-bromopropane.

  1. In propene the +I and hyperconjugation of CH₃ pushes π-electron density toward C-1 (the CH₂ carbon), so C-1 is δ⁻ and C-2 is δ⁺ even before reaction.
  2. The electrophile H⁺ attacks the electron-rich C-1; under the +E effect the π electrons move to C-1 and the positive charge appears on C-2, giving the secondary cation CH₃–CH⁺–CH₃.
  3. Br⁻ then attaches to the cation: 2-bromopropane is the major product (Markovnikov addition).
propene 2-bromopropane (major) 1-bromopropane (minor)
Illustration 7.3 Adv

Which statement is true?

(A) Electromeric effect is a permanent effect. (B) The electromeric effect operates in the ground state. (C) Electromeric effect involves complete transfer of π-electrons. (D) The electromeric effect is observed in alkanes.

  1. (A) false (temporary); (B) false (only in the presence of the reagent); (C) true; (D) false (needs a multiple bond).
  2. Answer: C.

8. The mesomeric (resonance) effect

8.1 What it is

A mesomeric effect (M, also written R) is the permanent polarisation transmitted through a conjugated π-system by the delocalisation of π-electrons or of a lone pair. Unlike the inductive effect it does not fade with every bond: it is carried along the conjugated path and alters the electron density at alternate atoms of the chain or ring.

  • +M (+R): the group donates electrons into the π-system. The atom attached to the π-system has a lone pair (or a negative charge), which is pushed into the π-system. Examples: –NH₂, –OH, –OR, –O⁻, –NHCOCH₃, –X (halogen).
  • −M (−R): the group withdraws electrons from the π-system. The atom attached to the π-system is part of a multiple bond to a more electronegative atom (or carries a positive charge/empty orbital), and the π-electrons are pulled into it. Examples: –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COR, –COOH, –COOR, –SO₃H, –CONH₂.

IMP The test for the sign of M is always the same. Donor (+M): the first atom has a lone pair or a negative charge. Acceptor (−M): the first atom is doubly or triply bonded to a more electronegative atom, or is positively charged. Draw the curved arrow from the lone pair (or the π-bond) into the ring; the contributor you get tells you whether a negative or a positive charge appears on the ring.

8.2 Positions affected: ortho, para, not meta

The curved-arrow pushing of a donor on benzene places the negative charge at the ortho and para carbons of the ring; an acceptor places the positive charge at ortho and para (the meta carbons are skipped in every contributor). This is the reason ortho/para directors and meta directors exist in electrophilic substitution, and the reason ortho/para substituents change the acidity of phenols and benzoic acids much more than meta substituents.

+M of OCH₃: charge on o- and p-carbons⟶ +
Anisole: negative charge appears at the ortho and para carbons (contributors drawn: one ortho, one para)
−M of NO₂: charge on o- and p-carbons⟶ +
Nitrobenzene: positive charge appears at the ortho and para carbons

Most substituents show both effects. Their relative size decides the net behaviour.

Exam Trap Halogens are the exception to remember. For F, Cl, Br and I, the −I effect is stronger than the +M effect, so they make the ring less reactive than benzene (deactivating); but the +M effect, which operates only at the ortho and para positions, makes those positions less deactivated than meta, so they still direct o/p. For acidity of substituted benzoic acids and phenols the net effect of the halogen is electron-withdrawing at every position, with para weaker than meta because +M opposes −I most at para (e.g. p-chlorobenzoic acid pKₐ 3.99 vs m-chloro 3.83).

Direction of the mesomeric effect

Classify each group as +M or −M: –NHCH₃, –COCH₃, –Br, –CH=O, –OCOCH₃, –CN, –O⁻, –NO₂.

Illustration 8.2 Main

Drawing the contributors

Draw the resonance contributors that show the +M effect of the –NH₂ group in aniline (put the negative charge on the ortho and para carbons).

  1. The lone pair on N forms a C=N⁺ double bond. To keep the carbon (C-1) at four bonds one ring π-bond moves to the adjacent carbon, which becomes a carbanion (ortho). Repeating the shift places the carbanion at the other ortho carbon and at the para carbon.
  2. Hence the ring is electron-rich at the ortho/para carbons, and aniline brominates at these positions. Three negative-charge sites (o, o, p).
+M⟶ +
Aniline: lone pair of N pushed into the ring; negative charge at ortho and para
Illustration 8.3 Adv

Order of +M donor strength

Arrange the groups in decreasing +M effect: –NH₂, –OH, –F, –NHCOCH₃, –OCH₃, –O⁻.

  1. A lone pair on a less electronegative atom is donated more readily; a charged oxygen is a better donor than a neutral one; a lone pair already tied up with a carbonyl (amide, ester) is a weaker donor.
  2. –O⁻ > –NH₂ > –OCH₃ ≈ –OH > –NHCOCH₃ > –F. (In –NHCOCH₃ the N lone pair is shared with C=O, which makes it a weaker donor than –NH₂; fluorine is the most electronegative and holds its lone pairs most tightly, even though 2p–2p overlap with carbon is good.)
Illustration 8.4 Adv

Does acetophenone's carbonyl withdraw by M or I?

In acetophenone C₆H₅COCH₃ the carbonyl group deactivates the ring toward electrophiles. Show by resonance why meta substitution results.

  1. The ring π-electrons are pulled toward the carbonyl oxygen, leaving a positive charge on the ortho and para carbons; the meta carbons never become positive.
  2. An incoming electrophile is repelled from the (more positive) o/p positions and reacts at the least deactivated meta position.
−M⟶ +
Positive charge on the ortho and para carbons

8.4 Conjugation: three varieties and cross-conjugation

  • π–π conjugation: alternating double and single bonds (1,3-butadiene, benzene, acrolein CH₂=CH–CH=O). The delocalisation involves p-orbitals on adjacent π-bonds.
  • p–π conjugation (lone pair or empty p orbital next to a π-bond): vinyl chloride, aniline, allyl cation CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺, allyl anion, enolates.
  • σ–π conjugation (hyperconjugation): a C–H or C–C σ-bond adjacent to a π-bond, empty p orbital or radical (propene, toluene, ethyl cation).
  • Cross-conjugation: one atom/group is conjugated to two other π-systems that are not conjugated with each other. In divinyl ketone CH₂=CH–CO–CH=CH₂ and in benzophenone the carbonyl is conjugated with each vinyl or aryl group but the two do not communicate through the central carbon as well as through a linear chain; cross-conjugated systems delocalise less than linear systems.
1,3-butadiene (linear) acrolein divinyl ketone (cross-conjugated) benzophenone 1,3,5-hexatriene
Conjugated systems

8.5 Consequences of the mesomeric effect

  • Acidity of phenol and carboxylic acids: phenoxide and carboxylate are stabilised by delocalisation of the negative charge.
  • Basicity of amides, anilines: the lone pair on N is delocalised and so not available to bind H⁺.
  • Orientation in aromatic substitution.
  • Bond lengths: C–N in amides (133 pm) shorter than in amines (147 pm); C–O in phenol (136 pm) shorter than in methanol (143 pm); C–Cl in vinyl chloride (172 pm) shorter than in ethyl chloride (177 pm).
  • Dipole moments: the large dipole of p-nitroaniline (6.2 D) is more than the vector sum (5.5 D) because the +M of NH₂ and −M of NO₂ reinforce through the ring (push–pull).
  • Colour: extended conjugation shifts absorption to the visible (azo dyes, indicators like methyl orange, push–pull chromophores).
  • Reactivity of carbonyls: acid chlorides and aldehydes are reactive; amides and carboxylates are unreactive because the donor group conjugates with C=O.
Illustration 8.5 Adv

Push–pull

Explain why the C–N bond in p-nitroaniline has more double-bond character than that in aniline and why p-nitroaniline is a much weaker base than aniline.

  1. NH₂ is a +M donor and NO₂ a −M acceptor, placed at positions that are conjugated with each other (para). The lone pair on N can flow through the ring directly onto the oxygens of the nitro group (the quinoid contributor), giving the C–N bond extra double-bond character.
  2. The N lone pair is therefore delocalised more than in aniline, is less available for H⁺ and p-nitroaniline (pKₐ of conjugate acid 1.0) is a far weaker base than aniline (4.6).
push-pull⟶
p-Nitroaniline: the lone pair of NH₂ flows through the ring onto the nitro group

9. Resonance: rules, drawing and stability

9.1 The idea

When a single Lewis structure cannot describe a molecule, we draw two or more contributing (canonical) structures; the real molecule is a resonance hybrid, not an equilibrium between them and not an average in time — a single species whose structure is a weighted mixture. The contributors differ only in the positions of electrons (π-electrons and lone pairs), never in the positions of atoms. The double-headed arrow ↔ joins them; the equilibrium arrow ⇌ is for different molecules (tautomers, conformers).

IMP Resonance energy is the difference in energy between the real hybrid and the most stable contributor. It is large when (i) there are many contributors of similar energy, (ii) the contributors are equivalent (benzene, carboxylate), (iii) the orbitals overlap well (planarity).

9.2 The rules for writing resonance structures

  • Rule 1 — Only electrons move. The skeleton of σ-bonded atoms is fixed. Moving a hydrogen atom changes the compound (a tautomer), not the contributor.
  • Rule 2 — The number of paired and unpaired electrons is constant. All contributors have the same total charge and the same number of electrons.
  • Rule 3 — Only π-electrons and lone pairs move. σ-electrons stay (except in hyperconjugation, which is treated separately).
  • Rule 4 — Every atom stays within the valence limit. Second-row atoms (C, N, O, F) never exceed eight electrons. Counting electrons around each atom after each arrow is the best check.
  • Rule 5 — The contributing atoms must lie in one plane (or nearly so) so that their p-orbitals overlap; a bond that is twisted cannot take part (steric inhibition of resonance, treated in its own section below).

Curved arrows start at an electron source (a lone pair or a π-bond) and end at the place where the electrons will be (a new π-bond or a lone pair on the next atom); the tail never starts at an atom or at a positive charge.

9.4 Which contributor is more important? The ranking rules

When the contributors are not equivalent, the real structure resembles the most stable one. Compare them in this order:

  • 1. Octets: a structure in which all second-row atoms have a complete octet is better than one with a sextet. Example: CH₃–O⁺=CH₂ (all octets) is better than CH₃–O–CH₂⁺ (carbon has a sextet).
  • 2. Number of covalent bonds: more bonds (and more π-bonds) is better.
  • 3. Charge separation: fewer charges, or none, is better. A neutral structure beats a zwitterion; if charges are needed, the shortest separation, and opposite charges close together, is better.
  • 4. Charge on the right atom: a negative charge belongs on the more electronegative atom (O > N > C); a positive charge on the less electronegative atom.
  • 5. Aromatic (and non-quinoid) rings preserved: a contributor that keeps the benzene ring intact is better than one that disrupts it.
  • 6. Equivalent contributors: a set of equivalent contributors gives the greatest stabilisation.
Illustration 9.1 Main

Rank the contributors

Rank the contributors of CH₂=CH–CH=O (acrolein) in order of importance.

  1. I: all octets, no charges, three π/σ bonds as drawn — the major contributor.
  2. II: charge-separated but the negative charge is on O (more electronegative) and the positive on C; all atoms except the terminal carbon have octets (the cation has a sextet) — a significant minor contributor, and it explains why the β-carbon is electrophilic (Michael addition).
  3. III: negative on the less electronegative carbon and positive on oxygen, which would have only a sextet — it does not contribute.
  4. I > II ≫ III.
I (neutral) II (C⁺, O⁻) III (C⁻, O⁺ — absurd)
Illustration 9.2 Adv

Which contributor of the enolate is better?

For the enolate of acetone, compare CH₂=C(CH₃)–O⁻ with ⁻CH₂–C(=O)CH₃. Which is the more important contributor and which atom is the nucleophile in alkylation reactions?

  1. In the O⁻ form the negative charge is on oxygen (the more electronegative atom); in the C⁻ form it is on carbon but the structure has a strong C=O bond (more covalent energy).
  2. The two are of similar energy; the O⁻ form is slightly more important for the charge distribution (higher charge density on O), yet the C⁻ form is why the carbon of an enolate acts as the soft nucleophile (alkylation at carbon, aldol).
  3. In the hybrid the charge is shared between O and the α-carbon.
O⁻ form C⁻ form

9.5 Resonance energy and what it can be measured from

The resonance energy of a molecule is estimated from heats of hydrogenation (or of combustion). If benzene contained three isolated C=C bonds, hydrogenating it would release three times the heat released by cyclohexene. The measured values show how much more stable benzene is.

Heats of hydrogenation (kJ mol⁻¹, to the saturated hydrocarbon)
CompoundΔH(hyd) observedΔH expected for localised bondsStabilisation
Cyclohexene−120——
1,3-Cyclohexadiene−2322 × (−120) = −240≈ 8 (small conjugation)
Benzene−2083 × (−120) = −360≈ 152 (36 kcal mol⁻¹)
1,3-Butadiene (to butane)−2392 × (−127) = −254 (1-butene −127)≈ 15 (3.5 kcal mol⁻¹)
IMP The resonance energy of benzene (≈ 150 kJ mol⁻¹) is much greater than the conjugation energy of a diene (≈ 15 kJ mol⁻¹): aromatic stabilisation is a different order of magnitude. Resonance energies: benzene ≈ 150, naphthalene ≈ 255, anthracene ≈ 350, phenanthrene ≈ 380 kJ mol⁻¹; per ring the resonance energy decreases with fusion (benzene 150 per ring, naphthalene ≈ 128 per ring), so anthracene and phenanthrene undergo addition reactions more readily than benzene.
Illustration 9.3 Main

Resonance energy from heats of hydrogenation

ΔH(hydrogenation) of cyclohexene = −120 kJ mol⁻¹ and of benzene = −208 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the resonance energy of benzene.

  1. Hypothetical 'cyclohexatriene' with three isolated double bonds: ΔH = 3 × (−120) = −360 kJ mol⁻¹.
  2. Observed ΔH = −208 kJ mol⁻¹.
  3. Resonance energy = 360 − 208 = 152 kJ mol⁻¹ (benzene is 152 kJ mol⁻¹ more stable than the localised triene).
Illustration 9.4 Adv

Resonance energy of naphthalene

The enthalpy of combustion of naphthalene is −5156 kJ mol⁻¹, whereas the value calculated for a hypothetical localised Kekulé structure (from bond energies, taken as given) is −5411 kJ mol⁻¹. Calculate the resonance energy and compare it with benzene.

  1. RE = 5411 − 5156 = 255 kJ mol⁻¹.
  2. Naphthalene has two rings, so 255/2 ≈ 128 kJ mol⁻¹ per ring, about 85 % of the value for benzene (152): fused rings share their π-electrons, so each ring is slightly less aromatic. This is why naphthalene is more reactive than benzene in both substitution and addition.

9.7 Resonance, bond order and bond length

The bond order in the hybrid is the average of the bond orders in the contributors: carboxylate 1.5; nitrate N–O 1⅓; carbonate C–O 1⅓; benzene C–C 1.5; allyl C–C 1.5; ozone O–O 1.5; amide C–N between 1 and 2 (about 1.3–1.4). The bond lengths follow the bond orders; the experimental lengths (benzene 139 pm; carbonate 129 pm, between C–O 143 and C=O 122) confirm this.

Illustration 9.7 Adv

Bond order in nitrate

Calculate the N–O bond order in NO₃⁻ and the formal charge on each oxygen in the hybrid.

  1. Each contributor has two N–O single bonds and one N=O. The total number of N–O bond units is 4 spread over three bonds: bond order = 4/3 = 1.33.
  2. Each oxygen carries −1 in two contributors and 0 in one: average = −2/3. The hybrid has a charge of −⅔ on each O and +1 on N (total −1).
nitrate
Illustration 9.8 Adv

Compare C–O bond lengths

Arrange in increasing order of C–O bond length: CO₃²⁻, CH₃OH, CH₃COO⁻, CO₂, CH₃CHO.

  1. Bond orders: CO₂ (2, plus extra π because of two C=O: 116 pm), CH₃CHO (2, 121 pm), CH₃COO⁻ (1.5, 126 pm), CO₃²⁻ (1.33, 129 pm), CH₃OH (1, 143 pm).
  2. CO₂ < CH₃CHO < CH₃COO⁻ < CO₃²⁻ < CH₃OH.

10. Hyperconjugation

10.1 The idea

In hyperconjugation (also called σ–π conjugation or 'no-bond resonance') the electrons of a σ-bond, usually C–H of an alkyl group attached to an unsaturated carbon, are delocalised into the neighbouring empty or partially filled p-orbital or into the antibonding π* orbital. The σ-bond is said to 'conjugate' with the π-system without being a π-bond itself.

ethyl cation isopropyl cation tert-butyl cation propene toluene ethyl radical
The sp³ carbon next to the cationic, alkene or radical carbon bears the α-hydrogens
  • σ(C–H) → empty p-orbital (carbocation): stabilises the cation.
  • σ(C–H) → π\* (alkene): stabilises the alkene, makes the double bond a little longer and the adjacent C–C bond a little shorter.
  • σ(C–H) → half-filled p (radical): stabilises the radical.

For the C–H bond to overlap with the p-orbital, the bond must be roughly parallel to the axis of the p-orbital: free rotation of the CH₃ group provides it.

hyperconjugation⟶
Ethyl cation: H–C σ-electrons delocalise into the empty p orbital (no-bond structure written as H⁺ C=C, with the H–C bond broken only formally)
hyperconjugation⟶
Propene: no-bond structures H⁺ ⁻CH₂–CH=CH₂ ; the C=C then has partial single-bond and the C–CH₃ bond partial double-bond character
IMP Counting rule. The number of hyperconjugative (no-bond) structures = the number of α-hydrogens, i.e. the hydrogens on the carbons directly attached to the positively charged / sp² / radical carbon. More α-H ⟹ more hyperconjugation ⟹ more stable cation, radical or alkene.

Exam Trap The α-carbon must be bonded to the unsaturated carbon. Hydrogens on carbons farther away (β-hydrogens of a cation, the C–H of the CH₂ in CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ beyond the first carbon) do not count. In CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ the α-carbon is the CH₂ next to C⁺ and it carries 2 α-H; the CH₃ is a β-carbon. A carbon with no hydrogens (such as the central carbon of (CH₃)₃C–CH₂⁺) contributes none directly.

10.2 Evidence and applications

Heats of hydrogenation of alkenes (kJ mol⁻¹, approximate) — less exothermic = more stable alkene
AlkeneAlkyl substituentsα-HΔH hydrogenation
Ethene00−137
Propene13−126
1-Butene12−127
cis-2-Butene26−120
trans-2-Butene26−116
2-Methylpropene26−119
2-Methyl-2-butene39−113
2,3-Dimethyl-2-butene412−111

Alkene stability rises with the number of alkyl groups on the double bond: R₂C=CR₂ > R₂C=CHR > R₂C=CH₂ ≈ RCH=CHR (trans > cis) > RCH=CH₂ > CH₂=CH₂. This is the thermodynamic basis of the Saytzeff (Zaitsev) rule for elimination. The trans isomer is more stable than cis because of reduced steric repulsion (about 4 kJ mol⁻¹ in 2-butene), not because of hyperconjugation (both have six α-H).

  • Carbocations: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺ because of +I and hyperconjugation (9, 6, 3, 0 α-H).
  • Free radicals: 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃• (the same reasoning; C–H BDE of ethane 423, propane (secondary) 413, isobutane (tertiary) 404 kJ mol⁻¹).
  • Bond lengths: C(sp³)–C(sp²) in propene (150 pm) is shorter than in ethane (154 pm) and the C=C bond is slightly longer than in ethene — partly s-character but also partial double-bond character in the C–CH₃ bond.
  • Dipole moments: propene 0.36 D, toluene 0.36 D with CH₃ as the positive end.
  • Orientation in toluene: the CH₃ group (+I and hyperconjugation) activates the ring at ortho and para. p-Toluic acid (pKₐ 4.34) is a weaker acid than benzoic acid (4.20), because the methyl group donates electrons.
  • Carbanions are destabilised by alkyl groups (+I effect, and no π-acceptor help): CH₃⁻ > 1° > 2° > 3°.
Illustration 10.1 Main

Count the hyperconjugative structures

Count the number of hyperconjugative structures for (a) (CH₃)₂CH⁺, (b) CH₃CH=CH–CH₃, (c) 2-methylbut-2-ene (CH₃)₂C=CHCH₃, (d) toluene, and give the total.

  1. (a) two CH₃ on the cationic carbon: 6. (b) each CH₃ on the sp² carbons: 6. (c) three CH₃ groups on the sp² carbons: 9. (d) one CH₃ on the ring: 3.
  2. Total = 6 + 6 + 9 + 3 = 24.
Illustration 10.2 Main

Stability of alkenes

Arrange in increasing stability: 1-butene, trans-2-butene, 2-methyl-2-butene, cis-2-butene, 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene.

  1. More substituents on C=C ⟹ more α-H ⟹ more stable. Disubstituted trans is more stable than cis (less steric strain); monosubstituted 1-butene is the least stable.
  2. 1-butene < cis-2-butene < trans-2-butene < 2-methyl-2-butene < 2,3-dimethyl-2-butene (ΔH hyd: −127, −120, −116, −113, −111 kJ mol⁻¹).
Illustration 10.3 Adv

Hyperconjugation or induction?

The relative rates of reaction of p-alkylbenzyl bromides with a nucleophile follow the order p-CH₃ > p-C₂H₅ > p-iPr > p-tBu in some solvents (Baker–Nathan order), which is the order of the number of α-C–H bonds. In other solvents the order is reversed. What does this show?

  1. If hyperconjugation alone controlled the rates, the order would be the same in all media: CH₃ (3 α-H) > C₂H₅ (2) > iPr (1) > tBu (0).
  2. The reversal in other media (Hughes–Ingold order, tBu > iPr > Et > Me, the order of the +I effect) shows that the order depends on solvation of the alkyl groups: C–H bonds near the reaction site are solvated best when there are more hydrogens.
  3. Therefore the 'Baker–Nathan effect' is not a clean proof of hyperconjugation; for JEE Advanced you simply use: hyperconjugation counts α-H, inductive effect counts size, and both favour t-butyl for carbocation stability.
Illustration 10.4 Adv

Which carbocation is more stable?

Compare (CH₃)₃C⁺ and CH₃CH₂⁺ on (i) α-H count, (ii) inductive effect, and give the conclusion.

  1. (i) (CH₃)₃C⁺ has 9 α-H, CH₃CH₂⁺ has 3: nine hyperconjugative structures against three.
  2. (ii) Three methyl groups donate electrons by +I, one methyl donates less.
  3. Both effects stabilise the tertiary cation: (CH₃)₃C⁺ ≫ CH₃CH₂⁺ (in the gas phase the tertiary cation is far more easily formed from the hydrocarbon than the ethyl cation; in solution only 3° halides ionise readily in SN1).
Illustration 10.5 Adv

Bond length with hyperconjugation

Why is the C–C single bond in CH₃–CH=CH₂ shorter (150 pm) than in CH₃–CH₃ (154 pm)?

  1. Two effects: (1) the carbon of the CH=CH₂ is sp² (33 % s) and bonds formed from sp²–sp³ overlap are shorter than sp³–sp³; (2) hyperconjugation gives the C–CH₃ bond partial double-bond character through the no-bond structures H⁺ ⁻CH₂–CH=CH₂ ↔ H⁺ CH₂=CH–CH₂⁻.
  2. Both effects shorten the bond.

10.3 Negative hyperconjugation and reverse hyperconjugation

  • Negative hyperconjugation: donation from a lone pair (or a filled p-orbital) into an adjacent σ* orbital such as σ*(C–F) or σ*(C–O). It underlies the gauche preference of 1,2-difluoroethane and the anomeric effect in sugars (axial OR on the anomeric carbon of a pyranose is preferred) and helps explain why carbanions β to fluorine are stabilised.
  • Reverse hyperconjugation (σ* acceptance): the C–X bonds of –CF₃ and –CCl₃ are low-energy acceptors; they accept π-electron density from an adjacent π-system. This is invoked, besides the very strong −I effect, for the meta-directing nature and the strong deactivation by –CF₃ and –CCl₃ (σ* C–X orbitals) – the groups behave as 'electron acceptors' without a π-bond.
Illustration 10.6 Adv

Direction of the dipole moment

In 3,3,3-trifluoropropene CF₃–CH=CH₂ the C=C bond is polarised by the CF₃ group. Name the electronic effects responsible and state which alkene carbon becomes δ⁺.

  1. CF₃ is a very strong −I group and also an acceptor through σ*(C–F) (reverse hyperconjugation), withdrawing electron density from the double bond, so the C=C carbon next to CF₃ is δ⁺.
  2. The CH carbon attached to CF₃ is therefore δ⁺ and the terminal =CH₂ carbon is δ⁻ (how this C=C polarisation combines with the C–F bond dipoles to give the net molecular dipole is not asked here).

Summary sheet: electronic effects

IMP Summary sheet — Inductive, mesomeric, electromeric, hyperconjugation.
  • Inductive: σ-bonds, permanent, decays rapidly, depends on electronegativity and s-character.
  • Mesomeric: π or lone pair conjugated, permanent, alternate positions, does not decay with distance but needs planarity.
  • Electromeric: one multiple bond, temporary, reagent needed.
  • Hyperconjugation: σ(C–H) next to π, p, or radical; the number of hyperconjugative structures equals the number of α-hydrogens.
  • +M groups: –O⁻ > –NR₂ > –NH₂ > –OH ≈ –OR > –NHCOR > –OCOR > halogens.
  • −M groups: –NO₂ > –CN ≈ –SO₃H > –CHO > –COR > –COOH ≈ –COOR > –CONH₂ > –COO⁻.
  • When −I and +M oppose, +M wins for –OH, –OR, –NH₂ (activating) and −I wins for halogens (deactivating).
  • Resonance requires planarity; a twisted donor/acceptor loses its M effect (SIR).

12. Aromaticity, anti-aromaticity and non-aromaticity

12.1 The four conditions and the Hückel rule

A ring is aromatic if and only if it satisfies all four of the following conditions. Fail any one and the ring is not aromatic.

  • 1. Cyclic. The π-electrons must circulate round a closed loop.
  • 2. Planar (or very nearly planar), so that the p-orbitals on all ring atoms are parallel and overlap continuously.
  • 3. Completely conjugated: every ring atom must have a p-orbital that is part of the π-system (no sp³ atoms in the ring). Ring atoms may contribute 0 (empty p), 1 (one electron in a double bond or a radical) or 2 electrons (a lone pair in a p-orbital).
  • 4. Contains (4n + 2) π-electrons (n = 0, 1, 2, 3, …): 2, 6, 10, 14, 18 …. This is the Hückel rule.

A ring that satisfies 1–3 but has 4n π-electrons (4, 8, 12 …) is anti-aromatic: it is less stable than the open-chain analogue, and the molecule distorts (non-planar or bond-localised) to escape the destabilisation. A ring that fails condition 1, 2 or 3 is non-aromatic; its stability is normal.

Summary of the three classes
ClassCyclic, planar, fully conjugated?π-electronsEnergyExamples

Non-aromaticno (a ring atom is sp³, or the ring is not planar)anynormalcyclohexene, cyclopentadiene, cyclooctatetraene (tub)

Illustration 12.1 Main

Classify each ring

Classify each as aromatic, anti-aromatic or non-aromatic and give π-electron count: (a) cyclopentadienyl cation (b) cyclopentadienyl anion (c) tropylium cation (d) cyclopropenyl cation (e) cycloheptatriene.

  1. (a) 2 C=C (4 e⁻) + empty p (0) = 4π, cyclic, planar, conjugated: anti-aromatic (4n, n = 1).

  5. (e) the CH₂ is sp³: the ring is not completely conjugated: non-aromatic.
Cp⁺ Cp⁻ tropylium cyclopropenyl⁺ cycloheptatriene

12.2 Why 4n + 2: a picture of the orbitals

For a planar cyclic array of N p-orbitals the π molecular orbitals form a pattern (Frost circle): one lowest-energy orbital, then pairs of degenerate orbitals, and (for even N) one highest orbital. A closed shell, with every bonding orbital filled and no electron in the non-bonding or antibonding orbitals, requires 2 electrons for the lowest orbital plus 4 for each degenerate pair: 2, 6, 10, 14 … = 4n + 2. With 4n electrons the last pair of electrons must enter a degenerate set of non-bonding orbitals, one electron each (a diradical, Hund's rule), a very unstable arrangement — this is anti-aromaticity.

Benzene π molecular orbitals (Hückel energies in units of β; α is the energy of an isolated p-orbital)
OrbitalEnergyOccupation in benzene
ψ₆α − 2βempty (antibonding)
ψ₄, ψ₅α − β (degenerate)empty (antibonding)
ψ₂, ψ₃α + β (degenerate)filled (bonding)
ψ₁α + 2βfilled (bonding)

Total π energy of benzene = 2(α + 2β) + 4(α + β) = 6α + 8β. Three isolated ethene π bonds would give 3 × 2(α + β) = 6α + 6β. The difference, 2β, is the delocalisation (resonance) energy in Hückel theory; with β ≈ −75 kJ mol⁻¹ this is about 150 kJ mol⁻¹, in agreement with the thermochemical value in Section 9.5.

Illustration 12.2 Adv

Hückel energy of cyclobutadiene

For cyclobutadiene the Hückel π energies are α + 2β, α, α, α − 2β. Compare the delocalisation energy with that of two isolated ethene π-bonds.

  1. Four π-electrons: two in α + 2β, one each in the two degenerate non-bonding orbitals (energy α). Total = 2(α + 2β) + 2α = 4α + 4β.
  2. Two isolated π-bonds: 2 × 2(α + β) = 4α + 4β.
  3. The delocalisation energy is zero — and the molecule has two unpaired electrons in a planar square structure, so it is unstable (distortion to a rectangle gives some stabilisation). Hence cyclobutadiene is not stabilised, in sharp contrast to benzene (2β).

12.3 The annulene series

An annulene is a fully conjugated monocyclic hydrocarbon C_nH_n (n even) with alternating double and single bonds, named [n]annulene.

Exam Trap Hückel's rule says nothing about stability if the ring cannot become planar. Cyclooctatetraene (8π) is non-aromatic, not anti-aromatic, because it adopts the tub shape (a non-planar conformation, so the p-orbitals do not overlap continuously) and avoids the destabilisation; the same applies to [10]-, [12]- and [16]annulene. In JEE answer 'non-aromatic' for COT unless the question says 'planar'. Its dianion (10π) and dication (6π), however, are planar and aromatic.

Anti-aromatic ions and rings
  • Evidence for the aromatic ions: tropylium bromide (C₇H₇⁺Br⁻) is an ionic solid that dissolves in water, in contrast to ordinary alkyl bromides; the cyclopropenyl cation forms isolable salts (triphenylcyclopropenium bromide is stable); the cyclopentadienyl anion is formed with unusual ease (pKₐ of cyclopentadiene is 16, as acidic as water, whereas an alkane has pKₐ ≈ 50): ferrocene is made from it.
  • Evidence for anti-aromaticity: the cyclopentadienyl cation is so unstable that it cannot be generated from cyclopentadienyl halides by ionisation; the 4π cyclopropenyl anion is not observed as a stable species, whereas the 2π cation is.
Illustration 12.3 Main

Acidity of cyclopentadiene vs cycloheptatriene

Cyclopentadiene (pKₐ 16) is about 20 pKₐ units more acidic than cycloheptatriene (pKₐ 36) although both give a conjugated carbanion. Explain.

  1. Removing H⁺ from the CH₂ of cyclopentadiene gives the cyclopentadienyl anion: 5 carbons, 6π electrons, planar, cyclic, conjugated — aromatic, a very stable anion.
  2. Removing H⁺ from cycloheptatriene gives the cycloheptatrienyl anion: 7 carbons, 8π electrons: anti-aromatic and therefore destabilised (it is even less stable than a simple allyl-type carbanion).
  3. Conversely, cycloheptatriene readily loses hydride to give the aromatic tropylium cation, whereas cyclopentadiene does not lose hydride to give the anti-aromatic Cp⁺.
cyclopentadiene cycloheptatriene
Illustration 12.4 Adv

Which ion forms more easily

Predict which in each pair is formed more easily (more stable): (a) C₅H₅⁺ vs C₇H₇⁺ (b) C₅H₅⁻ vs C₇H₇⁻ (c) C₃H₃⁺ vs C₃H₃⁻ (d) C₄H₄²⁺ vs C₄H₄²⁻ (for (d) only state whether each ion obeys the 4n + 2 rule; no ranking is required).

  1. (a) C₇H₇⁺ (6π aromatic) vs C₅H₅⁺ (4π anti). Tropylium.
  2. (b) C₅H₅⁻ (6π aromatic) vs C₇H₇⁻ (8π anti). Cyclopentadienyl anion.
  3. (c) C₃H₃⁺ (2π aromatic) vs C₃H₃⁻ (4π anti). The cation.
  4. (d) C₄H₄²⁺ (2π) and C₄H₄²⁻ (6π) are both aromatic (4n + 2 with n = 0 and 1); both are known in special conditions; the dication is the more electron-poor, so which is 'easier' depends on the medium — they are both stabilised relative to the neutral anti-aromatic C₄H₄.

12.5 Heterocycles

In a heterocycle the heteroatom's contribution to the π-system depends on its role.

  • Pyrrole-type atom (N–H, O, S with two σ-bonds in the ring): the lone pair sits in a p-orbital and is counted (2 e⁻); the other lone pair of O and S (the second one) lies in the plane and is not counted.
  • Pyridine-type atom (N with one double bond, two σ-bonds in the ring): contributes 1 e⁻ to the π-system; the in-plane lone pair is not part of it and is free to be protonated.

Illustration 12.5 Main

Basicity from aromaticity

Why is pyridine (pKₐ of conjugate acid 5.2) a base while pyrrole (pKₐ of conjugate acid ≈ −3.8, protonated on carbon) is not?

  1. In pyridine the nitrogen is sp², its lone pair lies in the plane of the ring and is not part of the aromatic sextet. Protonation leaves the sextet intact (pyridinium is still aromatic).
  2. In pyrrole the nitrogen's lone pair is one of the six π-electrons. Protonating N would take the lone pair out of the ring and destroy the aromatic sextet; hence it is not basic (protonation, in strong acid, occurs at C-2 and gives a non-aromatic cation).
Illustration 12.6 Adv

Electron count in furan

How many π electrons does furan have, which lone pair of oxygen is included, and in which orbital is the other one?

  1. Furan: two C=C bonds (4 π e⁻) + one lone pair of O in a p-orbital (2 e⁻) = 6π.
  2. The second lone pair of oxygen is in an sp² orbital lying in the plane of the ring (perpendicular to the π cloud, not counted).
furan

  3. (c) benzene ring 6π + pyrrole C=C (2) + N lone pair (2) = 10π, aromatic.

12.7 Rings with exocyclic double bonds: carbonyls, fulvenes and quinones

  • Rule: treat a ring carbon bearing an exocyclic C=O (or C=C polarised toward the electronegative end) as carrying a positive charge with an empty p orbital: the ring has the π-count of the 'ring cation' resonance form. If that ring cation form is aromatic the compound is stabilised and polar; if anti-aromatic the compound is destabilised.
cyclopropenone (2π ring) cyclopentadienone (4π ring) tropone (6π ring) p-benzoquinone (non-aromatic) 6,6-dimethylfulvene azulene
Ring systems with C=O or exocyclic C=C
  • Cyclopropenone: the C⁺–O⁻ form has the aromatic 2π cyclopropenyl cation in its ring; the compound is unusually stable and polar (μ = 4.4 D).
  • Cyclopentadienone: the C⁺–O⁻ form has the anti-aromatic 4π Cp⁺ ring; the ketone is unstable and dimerises rapidly even at low temperature.
  • Tropone: the polar form has the aromatic tropylium ring (6π); tropone is polar, stable, basic at O (protonation gives hydroxytropylium).
  • Fulvene (pentafulvene, C₆H₆): the dipolar form would have an aromatic Cp⁻ ring and a carbocation on the exocyclic carbon; the molecule is only weakly polar and non-aromatic overall; donor groups on the exocyclic carbon (for example 6,6-bis(dimethylamino)fulvene) increase the polarity.
  • p-Benzoquinone: the six-membered ring has two C=O and two C=C: not aromatic (cross-conjugated diketone); it is a good oxidising agent because reduction gives the aromatic hydroquinone.
Illustration 12.8 Adv

Stability order

Arrange in decreasing stability (or aromatic character): tropone, cyclopentadienone, cyclopropenone, cyclobutadiene.

  1. Cyclopropenone (2π ring cation, stable, isolable) and tropone (6π ring cation, stable) are stabilised by aromatic dipolar structures. Cyclopentadienone (4π) is anti-aromatic and cyclobutadiene (4π) is anti-aromatic and the least stable of all.
  2. Tropone ≈ cyclopropenone > cyclopentadienone > cyclobutadiene (the last two undergo spontaneous dimerisation).

Order of resonance energy

Arrange in decreasing resonance energy: benzene, thiophene, pyrrole, furan.

  1. Resonance energies (kcal mol⁻¹): benzene 36, thiophene 29, pyrrole 21, furan 16. The more electronegative the heteroatom, the more tightly it holds its lone pair and the less it delocalises it. S is less electronegative than N, and N than O.
  2. benzene > thiophene > pyrrole > furan. Their reactivity toward electrophiles (EAS) is the reverse: pyrrole > furan > thiophene > benzene.

13. Acidity: the complete treatment

13.1 Definitions and the pKₐ scale

  • Brønsted–Lowry acid: a proton donor. Base: a proton acceptor. HA + B ⇌ A⁻ + BH⁺. Every acid has a conjugate base; the stronger the acid, the weaker (and more stable) its conjugate base.
  • Lewis acid: an electron-pair acceptor (BF₃, AlCl₃, H⁺, carbocations, SO₃); Lewis base: an electron-pair donor (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, R⁻, alkenes).

For HA + H₂O ⇌ A⁻ + H₃O⁺: K_a = [A⁻][H₃O⁺]/[HA] and pK_a = −log K_a. A lower pKₐ means a stronger acid; a change of one pKₐ unit is a factor of 10 in K_a. The pKₐ is the pH at which the acid is exactly half ionised (Henderson–Hasselbalch: pH = pKₐ + log [A⁻]/[HA]).

Formula Equilibrium constant for HA + B⁻ ⇌ A⁻ + HB : K = K_a(HA)/K_a(HB) = 10^(pKₐ(HB) − pKₐ(HA)). The reaction goes forward (product favoured) when HA is the stronger acid, i.e. when the acid on the left has the lower pKₐ.

Exam Trap Water cannot hold a base stronger than OH⁻ (the levelling effect): NaNH₂, NaH, RLi, RMgX react completely with water to give OH⁻ and so cannot be used in aqueous solution. For the same reason, acids stronger than H₃O⁺ (HCl, HClO₄, HNO₃) all appear equally strong in water; their order is established in non-aqueous solvents or from gas-phase data.

13.2 The four questions that rank any set of acids

Acidity is decided by the stability of the conjugate base A⁻ (and to a lesser extent by the stability of HA). Ask, in this order:

  • A — Atom: On which atom is the negative charge? Compare the atoms bearing the charge: electronegativity (across a period) and size (down a group). *This is decisive when the atoms differ.*
  • R — Resonance: Is the charge delocalised by resonance (carboxylate, phenoxide, enolate, nitronate, aromatic anions)? More equivalent, better-stabilised contributors = more stable A⁻.
  • I — Induction: Do −I groups (halogens, NO₂, CN, C=O, N⁺R₃, sp-carbons) withdraw electrons and stabilise A⁻? Does +I (alkyl) destabilise it? The effect falls off with distance.
  • O — Orbital (hybridisation): In which orbital does the lone pair sit? More s-character = more stable A⁻ (sp > sp² > sp³).

Then check the secondary effects: solvation of the anion (small, localised anions are solvated best in protic solvents), intramolecular H-bonding, steric hindrance to solvation, steric inhibition of resonance, ring strain, aromaticity.

IMP When two factors conflict, resonance beats induction, and a change of atom beats everything. CH₃COOH (pKₐ 4.8; O⁻ with resonance) is far more acidic than CF₃CH₂OH (12.4; O⁻ with three F but no resonance). H₂S (7.0) is more acidic than H₂O (15.7) although O is more electronegative: size dominates down a group. Across a period electronegativity dominates: acidity increases CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF.

  • Across a period the charge is placed on a more electronegative atom, which holds it better: C⁻ < N⁻ < O⁻ < F⁻. Acidity: CH₄ < NH₃ < H₂O < HF.
  • Down a group the anion is larger, the charge is spread over a larger volume (lower charge density) and the H–X bond is longer and weaker: HF < HCl < HBr < HI; H₂O < H₂S < H₂Se; ROH < RSH (CH₃OH 15.5, CH₃SH 10.3); PhOH 10 vs PhSH 6.6.
Exam Trap The factor that decides down a group is bond strength/size, not electronegativity. This is why HI is the strongest of the hydrohalic acids (weakest H–X bond) although F is the most electronegative halogen. Conversely, the strong C–F bond means H–F is a weak acid in water (3.2) partly because the small F⁻ is also extensively hydrogen-bonded and HF forms strong H–F···F⁻ (HF₂⁻) ions.

The more s-character in the orbital that holds the lone pair, the closer the electrons are to the nucleus and the more stable the anion. Cyclopropane (46) has C–H bonds of higher s-character (close to sp², ~33 %) than ethane. Alkyne protons are acidic enough to be removed by NaNH₂ (pKₐ NH₃ = 38) but not by NaOH or NaOEt (pKₐ ≈ 16): this is the standard method of forming acetylides.

Illustration 13.3 Main

Reaction of acetylene

Which of the following bases can convert HC≡CH (pKₐ 25) quantitatively into HC≡C⁻: NaOH, NaOC₂H₅, NaNH₂, Na₂CO₃? Calculate K for the reaction with NaNH₂.

  1. A base works if the conjugate acid of the base has a higher pKₐ than 25: NH₃ (38) qualifies; H₂O (15.7), C₂H₅OH (15.9), HCO₃⁻ (10.3) do not.
  2. HC≡CH + NH₂⁻ ⇌ HC≡C⁻ + NH₃: K = 10^(38 − 25) = 10¹³. With OH⁻: K = 10^(15.7 − 25) = 10^(−9.3) ≈ 5 × 10⁻¹⁰.
  3. Only NaNH₂.

13.5 Resonance: why RCOOH ≫ ROH and PhOH ≫ cyclohexanol

ethanol (pKₐ 15.9) acetic acid (4.76) phenol (9.99) cyclohexanol (16–18)
Resonance stabilisation of the conjugate base decides: carboxylate and phenoxide are resonance-stabilised, ethoxide and cyclohexoxide are not

In ethoxide the charge is localised on one oxygen. In acetate it is shared equally by two oxygens (two equivalent contributors). In phenoxide it is shared between oxygen and the ortho and para carbons (five contributors), but the contributors with the charge on carbon are less important, so phenoxide is stabilised less than carboxylate: RCOOH (pKₐ 4–5) > PhOH (10) ≫ ROH (16–18). Phenol is acidic enough to dissolve in aqueous NaOH, not in NaHCO₃; carboxylic acids dissolve in NaHCO₃ (evolving CO₂).

IMP Test for the acid strength of RCOOH, phenol, alcohol and water, used in analysis: the order RCOOH > H₂CO₃ > PhOH > H₂O > ROH > HC≡CH > NH₃ > alkanes. Hence RCOOH reacts with NaHCO₃ (gives CO₂); phenol does not; phenol reacts with NaOH, not with NaHCO₃; ROH reacts with Na, not with NaOH; alkynes react with NaNH₂, not NaOH.
Illustration 13.4 Main

Which dissolve in NaHCO₃?

Classify each compound as (a) dissolving in aqueous NaHCO₃ with evolution of CO₂ or (b) dissolving in aqueous NaOH but not giving CO₂ with NaHCO₃ or (c) neither: benzoic acid, phenol, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, ethanol, acetic acid, p-nitrophenol.

  1. NaHCO₃ liberates CO₂ only from acids stronger than carbonic acid (pKₐ₁ 6.35). NaOH (conjugate acid water, 15.7) deprotonates anything with pKₐ well below 15.
  2. (a) benzoic acid (4.20), acetic acid (4.76), 2,4,6-trinitrophenol (0.38).
  3. (b) phenol (9.99) and p-nitrophenol (7.15 — weaker than carbonic acid, so no useful reaction with bicarbonate).
  4. (c) ethanol (15.9) is not acidic enough to react with aqueous NaOH to any significant extent.
