Why is the C–H of nitromethane as acidic as phenol?

Nitromethane has pKₐ 10.2 and propane about 50. Explain with structures.

  1. Removing a proton from the carbon next to NO₂ gives a carbanion whose lone pair is conjugated with the N⁺=O: the charge is shared by carbon and two oxygens (nitronate ion, an analogue of the carboxylate).
  2. Propane's carbanion has no such delocalisation; its charge sits on sp³ carbon: pKₐ ≈ 50.

  • pKₐ₁ of a dicarboxylic acid is lower than that of the corresponding monocarboxylic acid because the second COOH is a −I group and because a statistical factor of 2 (two acidic groups) favours the first ionisation.

Illustration 13.8 Adv

Maleic and fumaric acids

Explain why maleic acid has a lower pKₐ₁ but a higher pKₐ₂ than fumaric acid.

  1. First ionisation: the maleate monoanion is stabilised by an intramolecular H-bond between the remaining COOH and the COO⁻ (they are held close by the cis double bond). Fumarate cannot form this bond. So H₂Mal → HMal⁻ is easier than H₂Fum → HFum⁻.
  2. Second ionisation: removing the H from the chelated HMal⁻ requires breaking that H-bond, and it creates two negative charges close together; the fumarate dianion has the charges far apart. So pKₐ₂(maleic) > pKₐ₂(fumaric).

13.8 Substituted benzoic acids

The benzoate anion is stabilised by −I and −M substituents and destabilised by +I and +M donors. Position matters: a *meta* substituent exerts essentially only its inductive effect; a *para* substituent exerts the inductive effect (weaker, because it is farther) and the resonance effect; an *ortho* substituent exerts both and, in addition, the special 'ortho effect' of Section 15.

IMP Compare every entry with benzoic acid, pKₐ 4.20. Lower pKₐ = stronger acid.
> Strong −I/−M groups (NO₂, CN): every position gives a stronger acid; the ortho isomer is strongest; para ≈ meta (3.44 and 3.45 for NO₂), because here −I (stronger at meta) and −M (only at para) compensate each other.
> Halogens (−I > +M): all positions are stronger than benzoic acid, except p-F which is nearly equal (4.14). The meta isomer is stronger than the para isomer: at para the +M effect opposes −I (m-Cl 3.83 < p-Cl 3.99).
> CH₃ (+I and hyperconjugation): the meta (4.27) and para (4.37) isomers are weaker acids than benzoic acid. The ortho isomer (3.91) is stronger: the ortho effect.
> OCH₃ and OH (+M and −I): at meta only −I operates, so m-OCH₃ (4.09) and m-OH (4.08) are stronger than benzoic acid. At para the +M effect wins, so p-OCH₃ (4.47) and p-OH (4.58) are weaker. At ortho both are stronger (o-OH, salicylic acid, 2.98, is boosted by an intramolecular hydrogen bond to the carboxylate).
Exam Trap The substituent effect on benzoic acids is much smaller than on phenols. In the benzoate anion the negative charge sits on the two oxygens, separated from the ring by the carboxyl carbon; it cannot be pushed directly into the ring. In the phenoxide ion the oxygen is attached to the ring and its charge is delocalised into the ring (o, p), so a para −M group such as NO₂ drops the pKₐ of phenol by 2.84 units (9.99 → 7.15) but that of benzoic acid by only 0.76 (4.20 → 3.44). In the language of Hammett: ρ(benzoic acids) = 1.0 by definition, ρ(phenols) ≈ 2.2.

Three methoxybenzoic acids

The pKₐ values of the three methoxybenzoic acids are 4.09 (ortho), 4.09 (meta) and 4.47 (para), and that of benzoic acid is 4.20. Explain.

  1. Meta: OCH₃ cannot donate by resonance to the carbon bearing COOH, so only its −I effect (oxygen is more electronegative than carbon) is felt: stabilises the anion; acid stronger than benzoic (4.09 < 4.20).
  2. Para: the +M effect pushes electrons toward the carboxyl-bearing carbon, opposing the −I effect and net destabilising the anion: weaker (4.47 > 4.20).
  3. Ortho: −I is strongest at the shortest distance and the ortho effect also operates: stronger (4.09).

Dinitro and trinitro compounds are stronger still: 2,4-dinitrophenol 4.09; picric acid 0.38 (as strong as many mineral acids).
↔⟶
The p-nitrophenoxide ion: charge delocalised onto the nitro oxygens through the ring
phenol (9.99) p-nitrophenol (7.15) 2,4-dinitrophenol (4.09) picric acid (0.38)
Acidity rises with the number of nitro groups at o/p positions
  • Alkyl groups (+I, hyperconjugation): destabilise the phenoxide: cresols (10.1–10.3) are weaker than phenol.
  • Halogens: −I > +M: all chlorophenols are stronger than phenol; o-Cl (8.56) > m-Cl (9.12) > p-Cl (9.41) (inductive effect falls with distance; +M opposes at p).
  • OCH₃: m-OCH₃ (9.65, stronger than phenol, −I) and p-OCH₃ (10.21, weaker, +M).
  • CHO, COCH₃, CN at para: −M: stronger acids (p-CHO 7.66, p-CN 7.97).
  • Steric inhibition of resonance: 3,5-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol (pKₐ 8.25) is a weaker acid than 4-nitrophenol (7.15) because the two methyl groups force the nitro group out of the ring plane, so it can no longer delocalise the negative charge by −M.
Illustration 13.13 Main

Rank the phenols

Arrange in increasing acidity: phenol, p-cresol, p-nitrophenol, m-nitrophenol, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.

  1. +I/hyperconjugation of CH₃ makes p-cresol (10.26) weaker than phenol (9.99). −M, −I of NO₂ at para (7.15) is stronger than −I alone at meta (8.39). Three NO₂ groups at o, o, p give picric acid (0.38).
  2. p-cresol < phenol < m-nitrophenol < p-nitrophenol < 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.
Illustration 13.14 Adv

Why is 3,5-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol less acidic than 4-nitrophenol?

Give the reasoning with the geometry of the nitro group.

  1. In 4-nitrophenoxide the NO₂ group is coplanar with the ring, so its π-bond is in conjugation with the ring and the charge of the phenoxide oxygen is delocalised onto the nitro oxygens.
  2. In the 3,5-dimethyl compound each methyl group is next to the nitro group and crowds it; the NO₂ is twisted about 90° out of the ring plane, its p-orbitals no longer overlap with those of the ring and the −M effect is lost (steric inhibition of resonance). Only the −I effect remains, together with the +I effect of two CH₃ groups.
  3. pKₐ 8.25 (vs 7.15): weaker acid.
4-nitrophenol 3,5-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol
Illustration 13.15 Adv

Phenols and the bicarbonate test

Which of these phenols can liberate CO₂ from sodium bicarbonate: phenol, p-nitrophenol, 2,4-dinitrophenol, picric acid? (pKₐ₁ of H₂CO₃ = 6.35)

  1. The reaction ArOH + HCO₃⁻ ⇌ ArO⁻ + H₂CO₃ (→ CO₂ + H₂O) is favoured only if pKₐ(ArOH) < 6.35.
  2. Phenol 9.99: no. p-Nitrophenol 7.15: no (K = 10^(6.35 − 7.15) = 0.16; incomplete, no effervescence). 2,4-Dinitrophenol 4.09: yes (K = 10^2.3). Picric acid 0.38: yes.

Illustration 13.16 Main

Water or tert-butyl alcohol?

Is tert-butyl alcohol a stronger acid than water in water? In the gas phase? Explain.

  1. In aqueous solution tert-butyl alcohol (pKₐ ≈ 18) is weaker than water (15.7): the three methyl groups push electrons toward O (+I) and the large tert-butoxide ion is poorly solvated by water.
  2. In the gas phase the order is reversed: tert-butyl alcohol is the stronger acid, because the alkyl groups polarise to stabilise the negative charge when no solvent molecules are available, so (CH₃)₃CO⁻ is more stable than HO⁻.

Strength of oxyacids

Arrange in increasing acid strength: HClO, HClO₂, HClO₃, HClO₄. Give two reasons.

  1. HClO < HClO₂ < HClO₃ < HClO₄.
  2. (i) More oxo oxygens give greater −I, which pulls electron density from O–H, loosening the proton. (ii) The conjugate base (ClO₄⁻ has four equivalent contributors; ClO⁻ only one) is more stabilised by resonance, and the charge is spread over more O atoms.

Cyclopentadiene versus cyclohexa-1,3-diene

Cyclopentadiene has pKₐ 16, whereas the CH₂ hydrogens of 1,3-cyclohexadiene are far less acidic (comparable with an allylic C–H of an alkene, pKₐ well above 30). Explain.

  1. Removing H⁺ from cyclopentadiene gives the planar 6π cyclopentadienyl anion, aromatic.
  2. Removing H⁺ from cyclohexa-1,3-diene gives a pentadienyl anion (6 π-electrons over 5 carbons in an open-chain-like conjugated system) with no aromatic stabilisation, just ordinary allyl-type delocalisation, so it is a much weaker acid.
cyclopentadiene 1,3-cyclohexadiene
Illustration 13.21 Adv

Acidity of nitroalkanes

Explain why the acidity increases in the order CH₃NO₂ < CH₃CH₂NO₂ < (CH₃)₂CHNO₂ although alkyl groups are +I.

  1. The nitronate ion (R₂C=N⁺(O⁻)O⁻) contains a C=N double bond. Alkyl substituents on the carbon of a C=N bond stabilise it by hyperconjugation (as in alkenes) — the more substituted the double bond, the more stable the ion.
  2. This stabilisation of the delocalised anion outweighs their +I destabilisation of the localised charge. pKₐ: 10.2 > 8.6 > 7.7.

14. Basicity

14.1 Measuring base strength

A base B takes up a proton: B + H₂O ⇌ BH⁺ + OH⁻, K_b = [BH⁺][OH⁻]/[B], pK_b = −log K_b. For comparison the pKₐ of the conjugate acid BH⁺ (written pKₐH) is used: pKₐH + pK_b = 14 in water at 25 °C. A higher pKₐH (lower pK_b) means a stronger base. Basicity is the exact reverse of the acidity of the conjugate acid: the more stable BH⁺ (the less willing to give up H⁺), the stronger the base.

  • What matters: the availability of the lone pair (or π-pair) for bonding to H⁺. Anything that lowers the electron density on the donor atom (−I, −M, delocalisation into a π-system or into a carbonyl, high s-character in the orbital holding the lone pair) weakens the base; anything that raises it (+I, +M of a substituent) or stabilises the conjugate acid (H-bonding to solvent, resonance in BH⁺) strengthens it.
The four questions to ask about a base
#QuestionEffect
1Which atom carries the lone pair?N is a better base than O (less electronegative, holds the lone pair less tightly): R₃N ≫ R₂O
2Is the lone pair delocalised (resonance) into a π-system or a carbonyl?delocalisation decreases basicity (aniline, amides, pyrrole)
3Hybridisation of the donor atomsp³ N (amines, 10–11) > sp² N (pyridine 5.2, imine ≈ 7 aq) > sp N (nitrile ≈ −10)
4Inductive and field effects, steric effects and solvation of BH⁺+I raises, −I lowers; in water, solvation of R₃NH⁺ reorders alkylamines

14.3 Aliphatic amines

  • Gas phase (no solvent): basicity increases with the number of alkyl groups, because alkyl groups stabilise the cation by +I and polarisability: R₃N > R₂NH > RNH₂ > NH₃. (In the gas phase proton affinities: NH₃ 854, CH₃NH₂ 899, (CH₃)₂NH 930, (CH₃)₃N 949 kJ mol⁻¹.)
  • Aqueous solution: the cation R₃NH⁺ is stabilised by hydrogen bonding to water: each N–H can donate a hydrogen bond. RNH₃⁺ has three N–H bonds (best solvated), R₂NH₂⁺ has two, R₃NH⁺ one. The loss of solvation with each added alkyl group opposes the +I effect and also bulk hinders solvation. The result is that the secondary amine is the strongest base for the methyl and ethyl series, and the tertiary amine is in the middle.
Aqueous basicity of methyl- and ethylamines (pKₐH)
SeriesNH₃RNH₂R₂NHR₃NOrder
R = CH₃9.2510.6410.739.80R₂NH > RNH₂ > R₃N > NH₃
R = C₂H₅9.2510.6510.9310.75R₂NH > R₃N > RNH₂ > NH₃
IMP The JEE rule for alkylamines in water. Methyl: secondary > primary > tertiary > NH₃ (Me₂NH > MeNH₂ > Me₃N > NH₃). Ethyl: secondary > tertiary > primary > NH₃ (Et₂NH > Et₃N > EtNH₂ > NH₃). For larger groups (R = C₂H₅ and above) the +I effect dominates over the small solvation difference, so 3° ≈ 2° > 1°; for large branched groups steric hindrance reduces everything. In non-aqueous solvents/gas phase the order is simply 3° > 2° > 1° > NH₃. Whenever a question gives no solvent, assume water and use the table above.

Arrange in decreasing basic strength in water: (CH₃)₃N, (CH₃)₂NH, CH₃NH₂, NH₃.

  1. pKₐH: (CH₃)₂NH 10.73, CH₃NH₂ 10.64, (CH₃)₃N 9.80, NH₃ 9.25.
  2. (CH₃)₂NH > CH₃NH₂ > (CH₃)₃N > NH₃. (+I increases basicity from NH₃ to the 2° amine; the 3° ammonium ion has only one N–H for hydrogen bonding with water and the 3° amine is more hindered, so it falls behind the 1° amine.)

Arrange in decreasing basic strength in water: (C₂H₅)₃N, (C₂H₅)₂NH, C₂H₅NH₂.

  1. pKₐH: (C₂H₅)₂NH 10.93, (C₂H₅)₃N 10.75, C₂H₅NH₂ 10.65.
  2. (C₂H₅)₂NH > (C₂H₅)₃N > C₂H₅NH₂. The larger +I effect of ethyl now outweighs the loss of solvation in going from primary to tertiary, but the hindrance prevents the tertiary amine from overtaking the secondary.
Illustration 14.3 Adv

Gas phase vs solution

In the gas phase the basicity order of the methylamines is NH₃ < CH₃NH₂ < (CH₃)₂NH < (CH₃)₃N, but in water the order of (CH₃)₃N and CH₃NH₂ is reversed. Explain.

  1. In the gas phase there is no solvent: each methyl group stabilises the ammonium cation by its +I effect and by polarisability, so basicity increases with the number of methyl groups.
  2. In water the ammonium ions are solvated by hydrogen bonds to N–H protons: RNH₃⁺ (3 N–H) > R₂NH₂⁺ (2 N–H) > R₃NH⁺ (1 N–H). The loss of stabilising solvation with each methyl group offsets the +I gain, so in water Me₃N is less basic than MeNH₂ and Me₂NH.

14.4 Aromatic amines: anilines

In aniline the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised into the ring (+M of NH₂); it is therefore less available than in methylamine and also its conjugate acid cannot enjoy the same delocalisation: aniline (pKₐH 4.60) is a much weaker base than aliphatic amines (about 10⁶ times) and weaker than NH₃.

  • EDG at o/p (+M, +I: CH₃, OCH₃) increases the basicity: p-toluidine (5.08) > aniline; p-anisidine (5.34).
  • EWG (NO₂, Cl, CN) decreases it: p-nitroaniline (1.00), m-nitroaniline (2.47), p-chloroaniline (3.98); the para −M group is much more effective than meta (NO₂ at para delocalises the lone pair through the ring onto the nitro group). m-Anisidine (4.20) is weaker than aniline because at meta OCH₃ is only −I.
  • Ortho substituent: o-toluidine 4.44, o-chloroaniline 2.65, o-nitroaniline −0.26 — in general every ortho substituent lowers the basicity of aniline (steric hindrance to solvation of the NH₃⁺ and to protonation; electrostatic effects), the 'ortho effect' of Section 15.
  • N-alkylation: N-methylaniline 4.85, N,N-dimethylaniline 5.07: modest increase (+I); but diphenylamine (0.78) and triphenylamine (≈ −5) show that a second and third phenyl drastically reduce the basicity because the lone pair is shared among several rings.
Exam Trap In N,N-dimethylaniline the NMe₂ group conjugates with the ring only if it can be coplanar. With a methyl group at the ortho position, steric inhibition of resonance twists NMe₂ out of the plane, the lone pair is no longer delocalised, and the base becomes stronger: 2-methyl-N,N-dimethylaniline is a stronger base than N,N-dimethylaniline (pKₐH about 5.9 against 5.1). Similarly, the ortho effect usually makes o-substituted anilines weaker, but SIR can reverse the trend: always check the geometry.
Illustration 14.4 Main

Aniline vs methylamine

Why is methylamine (pKₐH 10.64) a much stronger base than aniline (4.60)?

  1. In methylamine the lone pair is localised on N, enhanced by the +I effect of CH₃, and the ammonium ion is stabilised by solvation.
  2. In aniline the lone pair overlaps with the ring π-system (+M of NH₂) and is partly delocalised on the ortho/para carbons; it is less available for protonation. The anilinium ion has no such delocalisation (the lone pair is used for N–H), so protonation costs the resonance energy.
  3. Hence CH₃NH₂ ≫ C₆H₅NH₂ in basic strength.
methylamine aniline

  2. p-CH₃ > H > p-Cl > p-NO₂.

The ortho isomer is the weakest because the −I effect is strongest at the shortest distance, there is an intramolecular N–H···O–N hydrogen bond in the free base, and the ortho effect hinders solvation of the cation.
  3. aniline > m-NO₂ > p-NO₂ > o-NO₂.

14.5 Heterocyclic and special bases

pyridine (5.2) piperidine (11.1) pyrrole (−3.8) imidazole (7.0) DMAP (9.6) quinuclidine (11.0)
Nitrogen heterocycles
  • Hybridisation: pyridine (N is sp², 33 % s) pKₐH 5.2 vs piperidine (sp³, 25 % s) 11.1. The nitrogen lone pair in a more s-rich orbital is held more tightly.
  • Pyrrole (−3.8) is not basic: the N lone pair is part of the aromatic sextet. Protonation occurs on C-2 (not N) and destroys the aromaticity of the ring.
  • Imidazole (6.95): protonation at the pyridine-type N (N-3) gives the imidazolium ion in which the charge is shared equally by both nitrogens (two equivalent contributors); the pyrrole-type N–H lone pair is part of the sextet. Imidazole is much more basic than pyridine and the active-site histidine of enzymes. Pyrazole (2.5) is weaker because the two nitrogens are adjacent (−I of the other N, and the cation has less resonance stabilisation).
  • DMAP (9.6): the 4-dimethylamino group donates strongly (+M) through the ring to the pyridine nitrogen. DMAP is about 10⁴ times more basic than pyridine and a powerful acylation catalyst.
  • Quinuclidine (11.0) vs triethylamine (10.75): in quinuclidine the three alkyl arms are tied back in a bicyclic cage, so the lone pair is exposed and solvation is easy; no steric hindrance. DABCO (8.8) is less basic because of the second N.
  • 2,6-Di-tert-butylpyridine (3.58) is weaker than 2,6-dimethylpyridine (6.7) and pyridine (5.2): the bulky groups prevent solvation of the pyridinium N–H (hindrance to solvation).
  • Amidines and guanidines are the strongest neutral organic bases (acetamidine 12.4, guanidine 13.6) because the conjugate acid (amidinium, guanidinium) is resonance-stabilised: guanidinium has three equivalent contributors, the charge shared over three N atoms; the planar, symmetrical Y-shaped cation is exceptionally stable.
+H⁺⟶ +
Guanidine is protonated at the imino nitrogen; guanidinium: three equivalent contributors
  • Amides (acetamide −0.5) and urea (0.1) are very weakly basic: the lone pair on N is delocalised into C=O. They protonate at oxygen, not nitrogen, because the O-protonated cation is stabilised by resonance (the positive charge is shared with N).
  • Nitriles (acetonitrile ≈ −10): sp N, 50 % s-character: lone pair held very tightly.
  • Hydrazine (8.1), hydroxylamine (6.0): the α-effect: adjacent atom with a lone pair; their basicity is less than NH₃ though (inductive −I of the neighbour).
Illustration 14.8 Main

Pyridine and piperidine

Why is piperidine (pKₐH 11.1) 10⁶ times more basic than pyridine (5.2)?

  1. In piperidine the nitrogen is sp³ hybridised (25 % s-character) with a localised lone pair and the ring carbons are +I donors. In pyridine the nitrogen is sp² (33 % s): the lone pair is held closer to the nucleus and is less available; the N also experiences the −I effect of the ring sp² carbons.
  2. The difference of about 6 pKₐ units is 10⁶ in basicity.
Illustration 14.9 Adv

Which nitrogen of imidazole is protonated?

Explain which N of imidazole is protonated and why the cation is particularly stable.

  1. N-3 (pyridine-type, lone pair in plane) is protonated; its lone pair is not part of the aromatic sextet. The product has two N–H groups and the positive charge is delocalised between the two nitrogens (amidinium-type resonance: N–C=N⁺ ↔ N⁺=C–N). The two contributors are equivalent, which gives especially high stability (pKₐH 6.95).
  2. Protonating the pyrrole-type nitrogen N-1 would remove its lone pair from the 6π system, which is why this is not done.
+H⁺⟶
Imidazolium: both N atoms equivalent
Illustration 14.10 Adv

The strongest base

Which is the strongest base among: pyridine, aniline, guanidine, piperidine, acetamide? Why?

  1. pKₐH: guanidine 13.6, piperidine 11.1, pyridine 5.2, aniline 4.6, acetamide −0.5.
  2. Guanidine. Its protonation gives a resonance-stabilised cation with three equivalent contributors (positive charge on three N atoms), the highest stabilisation of the conjugate acid among these.

14.6 Arranging bases: a checklist

  • Step 1: Atom. Compare N, O, S, C bases by the atom carrying the lone pair. N > O.
  • Step 2: Delocalisation. A base whose lone pair is conjugated (amide, aniline, pyrrole) is weaker than one in which it is not (amine, pyridine). If the conjugate acid is stabilised by resonance (amidines), the base is stronger.
  • Step 3: Hybridisation. sp³ > sp² > sp.
  • Step 4: Inductive/steric/solvation effects in the same class.
HYF Anions as bases: the order of basicity is the reverse of the acidity of conjugate acids: NH₂⁻ > OH⁻ > F⁻; CH₃⁻ > NH₂⁻ > OR⁻ ≈ OH⁻ > CH₃COO⁻ > Cl⁻ > I⁻; R⁻ (alkyl) > R₂C=CH⁻ > RC≡C⁻ (carbanions: sp³ > sp² > sp). Bases that are very strong: R⁻ (alkyl-lithiums), NH₂⁻, H⁻, and RO⁻ among the oxygen bases.
Illustration 14.11 Main

Basic strength of anions

Arrange in decreasing basicity: CH₃COO⁻, OH⁻, CH₃O⁻, C₆H₅O⁻, Cl⁻. Use the aqueous conjugate-acid pKₐ values (H₂O 15.7, CH₃OH 15.5) to order OH⁻ and CH₃O⁻.

  1. The conjugate acid pKₐ: CH₃OH 15.5, H₂O 15.7, C₆H₅OH 10, CH₃COOH 4.76, HCl −7.
  2. OH⁻ ≳ CH₃O⁻ > C₆H₅O⁻ > CH₃COO⁻ > Cl⁻ (in water OH⁻ and CH₃O⁻ are close; the order OH⁻ > CH₃O⁻ follows the pKₐ of the conjugate acid).
Illustration 14.12 Adv

Basic strength of oxygen compounds

Why is dimethyl ether (pKₐH ≈ −3.8) a much weaker base than trimethylamine (9.8)?

  1. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so its lone pairs are held more tightly and the O–H⁺ bond formed is weaker; the oxonium ion is much less stable than the ammonium ion.
  2. The pKₐH of 10 and −3.8 reflect about 10¹³-fold difference in basicity.

15. Steric inhibition of resonance, the ortho effect and intramolecular hydrogen bonding

15.1 Steric inhibition of resonance (SIR)

Resonance needs the p-orbitals of the donor/acceptor group and of the ring to be parallel. If bulky neighbours force the group to rotate out of the plane of the ring, the overlap falls (it varies as cos θ, so it is zero at θ = 90°) and the mesomeric effect is lost or reduced. Only the inductive effect (which does not depend on geometry) remains. This is steric inhibition of resonance.

IMP SIR turns a +M or −M group into a purely inductive one. It therefore: raises the basicity of NR₂-substituted aromatics (the lone pair is no longer delocalised), lowers the acidity of phenols bearing a −M group (no delocalisation of the negative charge), raises the acidity of benzoic acids (the carboxyl group is no longer conjugated with the ring), and reduces the dipole moment of push–pull compounds.
4-nitro-N,N-dimethylaniline 2,6-dimethyl analogue (NMe₂ twisted) 3,5-dimethyl analogue (NO₂ twisted)
Methyl groups next to NMe₂ or NO₂ twist the group out of the plane
Standard SIR examples
SystemWithout SIRWith SIRObservation

Illustration 15.1 Main

3,5-Dimethyl-4-nitrophenol

Arrange in decreasing acidity: 4-nitrophenol, 3,5-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol, phenol, 3-nitrophenol.

  1. 4-Nitrophenol (7.15, −M, −I) > 3-nitrophenol (8.39, −I only) ≈ 3,5-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol (8.25; SIR eliminates −M, and the methyls are +I) > phenol (9.99).
  2. 4-nitrophenol > 3,5-dimethyl-4-nitrophenol ≈ 3-nitrophenol > phenol. (Exactly: 7.15, 8.25, 8.39, 9.99.)
Illustration 15.2 Adv

Basicity of N,N-dimethylanilines

Arrange in increasing basicity: aniline, N,N-dimethylaniline, N,N,2,6-tetramethylaniline. Explain the position of the last member.

  1. In N,N-dimethylaniline the NMe₂ group conjugates with the ring, but +I of the two methyls raises basicity a little above aniline.
  2. In N,N,2,6-tetramethylaniline two ortho methyl groups force the NMe₂ group perpendicular to the ring: the lone pair cannot overlap with the ring π-system and is as available as in an aliphatic tertiary amine (steric inhibition of resonance). It is the strongest of the three.
  3. aniline < N,N-dimethylaniline < N,N,2,6-tetramethylaniline.
aniline (4.60) N,N-dimethylaniline (5.07) N,N,2,6-tetramethylaniline
Illustration 15.3 Adv

Direction of the dipole and SIR

Why does 4-nitro-N,N-dimethylaniline have a much larger dipole moment than 2,6-dimethyl-4-nitro-N,N-dimethylaniline?

  1. In the planar molecule the +M of NMe₂ and the −M of NO₂ operate along the same axis through the ring (push–pull), giving a contribution of the charge-separated quinoid structure; the resulting extra charge separation increases μ.
  2. In the 2,6-dimethyl compound the two ortho methyl groups twist NMe₂ out of the ring plane, so its lone pair can no longer push through the ring; the push–pull contribution disappears and μ falls to the value expected from the σ-polarisation of the two groups alone. (Twisting the nitro group instead, with methyls ortho to NO₂, cuts the pull side and has the same kind of effect.)

15.2 The ortho effect in benzoic acids

Almost every ortho substituent — whether electron-donating or withdrawing — makes benzoic acid a stronger acid than expected from its electronic character, and usually stronger than benzoic acid itself.

Ortho effect in benzoic acids (pKₐ)
SubstituentorthometaparaComment
H (benzoic acid)4.20reference
CH₃3.914.274.37EDG ortho is stronger than benzoic acid
OCH₃4.094.094.47
NO₂2.173.453.44ortho ≫ para ≈ meta
Cl2.943.833.99
OH2.984.084.58intramolecular H-bond in the anion adds to the effect
2,6-(CH₃)₂3.25two ortho groups: bigger effect
2,6-(NO₂)₂1.14
IMP Explanation (JEE style). An ortho substituent twists the –COOH group out of the plane of the ring. This inhibits resonance between COOH and the ring — the ring can no longer donate electrons into the carbonyl by resonance. The carboxyl group becomes more electron-poor, its O–H bond is polarised more strongly, and the carboxylate anion is more stable relative to the acid. In addition, the ortho group exerts a −I effect that is strongest at this shortest distance, and (for OH, NH₂, NO₂) hydrogen-bonding or field interactions with the carboxylate.
Exam Trap 'All ortho-substituted benzoic acids are stronger than benzoic acid' is a good working rule for competitive exams; however, a few exceptions exist in the data (o-aminobenzoic acid, 4.98 in some sources). If a question lists o-NH₂ with a numeric pKₐ, use the number.
Illustration 15.4 Main

Ortho-toluic acid

The pKₐ of o-toluic acid is 3.91, m-toluic 4.27, p-toluic 4.37 and benzoic acid 4.20. Explain why o-toluic acid is stronger than benzoic acid although CH₃ is an electron-donating group.

  1. The methyl group at ortho forces COOH out of the plane (steric inhibition of resonance), which makes the acid stronger (ortho effect).
  2. The +I effect of methyl, which would decrease the acidity (as seen in the meta and para isomers, where there is no ortho effect), is outweighed.
Illustration 15.5 Adv

Order for chlorobenzoic acids

Arrange in decreasing acidity: o-chlorobenzoic acid, m-chlorobenzoic acid, p-chlorobenzoic acid, benzoic acid.

  1. o-Cl (2.94): −I strongest at ortho plus the ortho effect. m-Cl (3.83): −I only. p-Cl (3.99): −I weaker with distance and opposed by +M. Benzoic acid 4.20.
  2. o-Cl > m-Cl > p-Cl > benzoic acid.
Illustration 15.6 Adv

2,6-Dimethylbenzoic acid

Explain why the pKₐ of 2,6-dimethylbenzoic acid (3.25) is lower than that of o-toluic acid (3.91) and why 4-methyl-substitution has the opposite effect.

  1. Two ortho groups twist the COOH group by almost 90°: resonance with the ring is completely inhibited, so the effect is bigger than with one ortho methyl.
  2. A para methyl group has no steric interaction with COOH; it only donates electrons (+I, hyperconjugation) and weakens the acid (4.37 vs 4.20).
2,6-dimethylbenzoic acid o-toluic acid p-toluic acid

15.3 The ortho effect in anilines, phenols and pyridines

  • Anilines: every ortho substituent decreases basicity (usually more than the same substituent at para or meta, even for CH₃): o-toluidine 4.44 < aniline 4.60 although p-toluidine is stronger (5.08). The cause is steric hindrance to solvation of the NH₃⁺ group (and to the approach of H⁺) and the loss of coplanarity in the cation.
  • Phenols: o-alkyl phenols are slightly weaker than phenol (cresols 10.1–10.3); an ortho nitro or halogen is stronger by −I and −M. o-Nitrophenol (7.23) is not stronger than p-nitrophenol (7.15) because of intramolecular hydrogen bonding in the un-ionised molecule.
  • Pyridines: 2-substituents hinder N-protonation and N-alkylation: 2,6-di-tert-butylpyridine (3.58) cannot even be solvated normally and does not react with BF₃ (it is a hindered, non-nucleophilic base used to trap protons).
Illustration 15.7 Adv

o-, m-, p-toluidine

The pKₐH of o-, m-, p-toluidine are 4.44, 4.71 and 5.08 and aniline 4.60. Explain the order and why the ortho isomer is the weakest.

  1. p-Toluidine (5.08): +I and hyperconjugation of CH₃ at para, in conjugation with NH₂, raise electron density on N.
  2. m-Toluidine (4.71): only +I at meta (weaker, no hyperconjugation toward N).
  3. Aniline (4.60).
  4. o-Toluidine (4.44): +I would raise basicity, but the ortho effect (steric hindrance to solvation of the anilinium ion and to protonation) overrides it.
  5. p-Toluidine > m-toluidine > aniline > o-toluidine.

15.4 Intramolecular hydrogen bonding and its effects on acidity and volatility

Intramolecular hydrogen bonding happens when a donor (O–H, N–H) and an acceptor (O, N) are held about 5–6 atoms apart in the same molecule: the usual chelate ring is six-membered (five- or seven-membered chelates are also seen).

salicylic acid o-nitrophenol o-hydroxybenzaldehyde maleate monoanion acetylacetone (enol)
Molecules with intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bonds
  • Salicylic acid (2.98) vs 4-hydroxybenzoic acid (4.58) vs benzoic (4.20): in the salicylate ion the carboxylate oxygen is hydrogen-bonded to the ortho OH, a six-membered chelate that stabilises the anion. The effect on acidity is large. The second ionisation (phenolic OH, pKₐ₂ = 13.6) is very weak because the proton is held by the same hydrogen bond.
  • o-Nitrophenol: chelation in the neutral molecule makes it less acidic than expected (pKₐ 7.23 vs 7.15 for p). The hydrogen bond is in the acid; the proton is held back.
  • Volatility and solubility: o-nitrophenol (m.p. 45 °C, volatile in steam, soluble in non-polar solvents, poorly soluble in water) vs p-nitrophenol (m.p. 114 °C, involatile, intermolecular H-bonds, more soluble in water): steam distillation separates the two. Likewise o-hydroxybenzaldehyde (b.p. 197 °C) is more volatile than p-hydroxybenzaldehyde (m.p. 116 °C).
Illustration 15.8 Main

Salicylic acid

Salicylic acid is a stronger acid (pKₐ 2.98) than benzoic acid (4.20) and than p-hydroxybenzoic acid (4.58). Explain.

  1. Versus benzoic acid: OH is ortho, so it exerts a −I effect at the shortest distance; the ortho effect operates; and the salicylate anion is stabilised by an intramolecular O–H···O⁻ hydrogen bond (a six-membered chelate ring) between the phenolic OH and the carboxylate.
  2. Versus p-hydroxybenzoic acid: in the para isomer the +M of OH opposes the acid-strengthening effects and there is no chelation.
Illustration 15.9 Adv

o-Nitrophenol vs p-nitrophenol

Why is o-nitrophenol more volatile and less soluble in water than p-nitrophenol, and why is p-nitrophenol the stronger acid despite the ortho −I effect being stronger?

  1. Volatility/solubility: o-nitrophenol has an intramolecular hydrogen bond (O–H···O–N) so it does not associate with other molecules (or with water): low boiling point (relative to the para isomer), high vapour pressure, volatile in steam, lower solubility in water. p-Nitrophenol forms strong intermolecular H-bonds (with itself and with water): high m.p., not volatile, more soluble.
  2. Acidity: the chelated hydrogen of the ortho isomer is held back, so removing it requires breaking the H-bond; the stabilisation lost opposes the −I and −M gains. As a result pKₐ(o) = 7.23 > pKₐ(p) = 7.15: the para isomer is marginally stronger. Note the closeness of the values.

15.5 Steric inhibition of solvation and protonation

  • Steric inhibition of solvation (SIS): bulky groups hinder the solvent from stabilising an ion. Examples: tert-butyl alcohol (pKₐ 18) is a weaker acid than methanol in water; trialkylammonium ions are poorly solvated compared to primary ammonium ions; 2,6-di-tert-butylpyridine (3.58) is a weaker base than pyridine (5.23).
  • Steric inhibition of protonation (SIP): a hindered lone pair is hard to bind to a proton; in the extreme (2,6-di-tert-butylpyridine) the base does not react with larger acids (BF₃, CH₃I) though it takes up H⁺.
  • Bridgehead/Cage compounds: quinuclidine (11.0) is a better base than Et₃N (10.75) because the alkyl groups are tied back and cannot hinder the lone pair.
Illustration 15.10 Adv

Quinuclidine vs triethylamine

Quinuclidine is a stronger base (pKₐH 11.0) than triethylamine (10.75). What explains this and what does it say about the role of steric effects?

  1. Both are tertiary amines with sp³ N and three alkyl groups, so the electronic (+I) effect is the same. In triethylamine, free rotation about the C–N bonds lets the ethyl groups crowd round the lone pair, hindering solvation of the protonated N–H.
  2. In quinuclidine the three arms are tied back by the bicyclic cage, the lone pair is completely exposed, and the ammonium ion is well solvated. The difference is therefore a steric/solvation effect, not an electronic one.
quinuclidine triethylamine

16. Reactive intermediates and their stability

Most organic reactions proceed through short-lived species (carbocations, carbanions, radicals, carbenes, nitrenes, arynes) formed by bond fission. The stability of the intermediate decides the rate of its formation and therefore the product (Hammond postulate: the more stable the intermediate, the lower the energy of the transition state leading to it).

16.1 Bond fission and curved arrows

  • Homolytic fission: the bonding pair is split equally; one electron goes to each atom (radicals). Occurs in non-polar solvents, in the gas phase, with heat or light, or with radical initiators (peroxides). Written with fish-hook (half-headed) arrows.
  • Heterolytic fission: both electrons go to the more electronegative atom: cation + anion. Occurs in polar solvents and with acid/base catalysis. Written with full-headed arrows.

16.2 Carbocations

A carbocation has a positively charged carbon with six electrons, an empty p-orbital perpendicular to the plane of the three σ-bonds (sp², 120°). Its stability depends on how well the positive charge is dispersed.

Stabilising factors for carbocations (strongest first)

triphenylmethyl (trityl) cation diphenylmethyl benzyl allyl tert-butyl isopropyl ethyl methyl vinyl phenyl
Carbocations from the most to the least stable (conventional order)
IMP Order of carbocation stability (JEE convention): Ph₃C⁺ > Ph₂CH⁺ > PhCH₂⁺ ≈ CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ > 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺ > vinyl⁺ > aryl⁺. Remember also: a cation next to O or N with a lone pair (CH₃OCH₂⁺, R₂NCH₂⁺) is more stable than a comparable 3° alkyl cation; a 3° benzylic or 2° allylic cation is more stable than the corresponding primary benzylic/allylic cation (add the alkyl stabilisation on top of the resonance). Vinyl and aryl cations (the cationic carbon is sp-hybridised, the empty orbital in the plane) are extremely unstable.
Exam Trap Allyl vs benzyl vs tertiary. Resonance is generally a stronger stabiliser than hyperconjugation, so primary benzyl and primary allyl cations are placed above the 3° alkyl cation in the convention. (Real gas-phase and solvolysis data show the t-butyl cation is, in fact, comparable to the benzyl cation.) If a question lists both, follow the convention; if it compares a secondary allyl with a primary allyl, or a tertiary benzylic with a primary benzylic, the more substituted one is always more stable.
Illustration 16.1 Main

Rank the carbocations

Arrange in decreasing stability: (CH₃)₃C⁺, CH₃CH₂⁺, (CH₃)₂CH⁺, CH₃⁺.

  1. More alkyl groups give more hyperconjugation (9, 6, 3, 0 α-H) and more +I.
  2. (CH₃)₃C⁺ > (CH₃)₂CH⁺ > CH₃CH₂⁺ > CH₃⁺.
Illustration 16.2 Main

Compare allyl, benzyl and alkyl

Arrange in decreasing stability: C₆H₅CH₂⁺, CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺, CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺, (CH₃)₃C⁺, C₆H₅⁺.

  1. Benzyl: charge delocalised over seven atoms (CH₂ and the ortho, para carbons). Allyl: over three carbons. 3° alkyl: hyperconjugation. n-Propyl: little. Phenyl cation: empty sp² orbital in the ring plane, orthogonal to the π-system — no stabilisation.
  2. C₆H₅CH₂⁺ > CH₂=CH–CH₂⁺ > (CH₃)₃C⁺ > CH₃CH₂CH₂⁺ > C₆H₅⁺.
Illustration 16.3 Adv

Diphenylmethyl and an oxocarbenium

Which is more stable, CH₃O–CH₂⁺ or (CH₃)₃C⁺? Explain with resonance.

  1. In CH₃–O⁺=CH₂ every atom has an octet and there is a real C=O⁺ π-bond: strong stabilisation. (CH₃)₃C⁺ is stabilised only by hyperconjugation (9 C–H bonds). The oxocarbenium ion is the more stable.
↔⟶
The methoxymethyl cation: the oxygen lone pair fills the empty p-orbital; all atoms have octets in the left structure
Illustration 16.4 Adv

Para-substituted benzyl cations

Arrange in decreasing stability: p-CH₃O–C₆H₄–CH₂⁺, p-CH₃–C₆H₄–CH₂⁺, C₆H₅CH₂⁺, p-O₂N–C₆H₄–CH₂⁺.

  1. Electron-donating groups at the para position stabilise the benzyl cation: OCH₃ (+M, strong) > CH₃ (+I, hyperconjugation) > H; the nitro group destabilises (−M, −I).
  2. p-CH₃O > p-CH₃ > H > p-NO₂.

Rearrangements of carbocations

A carbocation rearranges when a 1,2-shift of H⁻ (hydride) or R⁻ (alkyl or aryl, with its bonding pair) can convert it into a more stable cation. The migrating group moves with its electron pair to the positive carbon.

1,2-H shift⟶
3-Methylbutan-2-yl (2°) → tert-amyl cation (3°)
1,2-CH₃ shift⟶
Neopentyl (1°) → tert-amyl (3°): a methyl group migrates
Illustration 16.5 Adv

Product of a rearrangement

When 3-methylbutan-2-ol is heated with concentrated HBr the main product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane. Explain.

  1. Protonation of OH and loss of water gives the secondary cation; the tertiary hydrogen on the neighbouring carbon shifts with its electron pair to the cationic carbon (1,2-hydride shift), forming the more stable tertiary cation; Br⁻ captures it.
HBr⟶ H shift⟶ Br⁻⟶
Protonation, loss of water, hydride shift, capture by bromide
Illustration 16.6 Adv

Bridgehead cations

Why is the 1-norbornyl (bridgehead) carbocation extremely unstable although it is tertiary?

  1. A carbocation wants to be planar (sp²) so that the empty p-orbital can be stabilised by hyperconjugation with three σ-bonds. At a bridgehead of a small bicyclic skeleton the carbon cannot flatten: the cage holds it pyramidal.
  2. The empty orbital therefore points away from the bonds and no effective hyperconjugation is possible: the cation is far less stable than an acyclic tertiary cation (1-bromonorbornane does not ionise under SN1 conditions).
norbornane 1-norbornyl cation

16.3 Carbanions

A carbanion has a carbon with three bonds and a lone pair (eight electrons), usually sp³ and pyramidal (like NH₃); when the lone pair is conjugated with a π-system or an electron-withdrawing group the carbon becomes sp² and planar. Carbanion stability is the reverse of the order for carbocations and parallels the acidity of the parent C–H (stronger acid = more stable carbanion).

  2. CH₃⁻ > CH₃CH₂⁻ > (CH₃)₂CH⁻ > (CH₃)₃C⁻.

sp, sp², sp³ carbanions

Arrange in decreasing stability: CH₃CH₂⁻, CH₂=CH⁻, HC≡C⁻.

  1. The lone pair is in an sp³ (25 % s), sp² (33 % s) or sp (50 % s) orbital; more s-character holds it closer to the nucleus. pKₐ of the parent C–H: 50, 44, 25.
  2. HC≡C⁻ > CH₂=CH⁻ > CH₃CH₂⁻.
Illustration 16.9 Adv

Stability of delocalised carbanions

Arrange in decreasing stability: (C₆H₅)₃C⁻, (C₆H₅)₂CH⁻, C₆H₅CH₂⁻, CH₃CH₂⁻, CH₂=CH–CH₂⁻.

  1. Delocalisation of the charge onto ortho and para positions of each phenyl ring: more rings, more delocalisation. (pKₐ of the parent C–H: Ph₃CH 30.6, Ph₂CH₂ 32, PhCH₃ 41, propene 43, ethane 50.)
  2. Ph₃C⁻ > Ph₂CH⁻ > PhCH₂⁻ > CH₂=CH–CH₂⁻ > CH₃CH₂⁻.

16.4 Free radicals

A free radical has an unpaired electron. Alkyl radicals are nearly planar (sp²) with the odd electron in a p-orbital, or very shallowly pyramidal; they are stabilised by hyperconjugation and by conjugation. The best guide to relative stability is the C–H bond dissociation enthalpy (BDE): the weaker the C–H bond, the more stable the radical produced.

Illustration 16.11 Adv

Major product of bromination

2-Methylpropane (isobutane) is brominated at 125 °C with Br₂/light. Which monobromide is the main product and why? What would chlorination give?

  1. Isobutane has 9 primary H and 1 tertiary H. For bromination the selectivity is about 1640 : 1 per H in favour of the tertiary H: ratio 1640 × 1 : 9 × 1, so the tertiary bromide is more than 99 % of the product: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane.
  2. For chlorination 5 × 1 : 9 × 1 gives about 36 % tertiary and 64 % primary chloride (1 : 3.8 : 5 per H): a mixture.
isobutane 2-bromo-2-methylpropane 1-bromo-2-methylpropane

16.5 Carbenes, nitrenes and arynes

  • Carbenes (:CR₂) have a neutral divalent carbon with six electrons. Singlet carbenes (paired electrons in one sp² orbital, an empty p-orbital) are electrophilic and add stereospecifically to alkenes to give cyclopropanes; triplet carbenes (two unpaired electrons, bent or linear) react in two steps as diradicals. Dichlorocarbene :CCl₂ (from CHCl₃ + KOH) is stabilised by the lone pairs on chlorine and is the electrophile in the Reimer–Tiemann reaction.
  • Stability of carbenes: stabilised by donor lone pairs and aromatic character: :CCl₂ and :CF₂ are more stable than :CH₂; N-heterocyclic carbenes (NHCs) are isolable.
  • Nitrenes (R–N:) are the nitrogen analogues with a sextet at N (generated from azides RN₃ by heat or light, with N₂ loss, and in the Hofmann, Curtius and Lossen rearrangements as the transient species).
  • Arynes (benzyne, C₆H₄): the 'triple bond' of benzyne is formed by sideways overlap of two sp² orbitals in the plane of the ring; it is highly strained and reactive; it is generated from o-halo-aryl halides with strong bases (NaNH₂), or by diazotisation of anthranilic acid, and is trapped by dienes (furan) and nucleophiles.
+ −H₂O, −Cl⁻⟶
α-elimination: chloroform and base give dichlorocarbene
+ ⟶
Dichlorocarbene adds to ethene to give 1,1-dichlorocyclopropane (concerted, stereospecific)
Illustration 16.12 Adv

Hybridisation of reactive intermediates

Give the hybridisation and shape of (a) CH₃⁺, (b) CH₃⁻, (c) •CH₃, (d) singlet :CH₂.

  1. (a) 3 σ-bonds, no lone pair, empty p: sp², trigonal planar (H–C–H 120°).
  2. (b) 3 σ-bonds + lone pair: sp³, pyramidal (like NH₃).
  3. (c) 3 σ-bonds + one electron in p: sp², planar (very slightly pyramidal in some radicals).
  4. (d) 2 σ-bonds + lone pair: sp², bent (H–C–H ≈ 102°).

Summary sheet: intermediates

IMP Stability orders in one place.
  • Carbocation: Ph₃C⁺ > Ph₂CH⁺ > PhCH₂⁺ ≈ allyl⁺ > 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃⁺ > vinyl⁺ ≈ aryl⁺; oxocarbenium and iminium ions are stabilised by the lone pair.
  • Carbanion: (delocalised onto O/N) > Ph₃C⁻ > PhCH₂⁻ > HC≡C⁻ > CH₂=CH⁻ > CH₃⁻ > 1° > 2° > 3°.
  • Radical: Ph₃C• > PhCH₂• ≈ allyl• > 3° > 2° > 1° > CH₃• > vinyl•.
  • s-character: more s ⟹ more stable carbanion, less stable carbocation.
  • Geometry: R₃C⁺ planar sp²; R₃C⁻ pyramidal sp³ (planar if conjugated); R₃C• planar/shallow-pyramidal; :CR₂ bent.

17. Tautomerism

17.1 What tautomers are

Tautomers are constitutional isomers that interconvert rapidly and spontaneously, usually by the migration of a hydrogen atom (as a proton) together with a shift of a double bond. Because the interconversion is fast (acid- or base-catalysed, or on mere standing), the isomers are in dynamic equilibrium and ordinarily cannot be separated. The commonest type is prototropic tautomerism.

IMP Tautomerism ≠ resonance. In resonance the same molecule is described by structures differing only in the positions of electrons (the hybrid is a single species, joined by ↔). In tautomerism two different molecules with different positions of an atom (H) are in equilibrium (joined by ⇌); they have different bond lengths, spectra and (often) reactivity.
Resonance vs tautomerism
FeatureResonanceTautomerism
What changespositions of electronsposition of a proton (atom) and a double bond
Number of speciesone (hybrid)two (or more), in equilibrium
Energyhybrid is more stable than any contributoreach tautomer is a real compound at an energy minimum
Symbol↔⇌
Detectable separately?noyes by spectroscopy; sometimes isolable

17.2 Keto–enol tautomerism

A carbonyl compound with at least one α-hydrogen (H on the sp³ carbon next to C=O) is in equilibrium with its enol (C=C–OH) form.

⇌⟶
Acetone (keto) and its enol (prop-1-en-2-ol): the equilibrium lies far on the keto side
  • Mechanism, base-catalysed: (1) the base removes the α-H giving the enolate ion (resonance-stabilised); (2) the enolate is protonated on O to give the enol (or on C to return to the keto form).
  • Mechanism, acid-catalysed: (1) protonation of the carbonyl oxygen; (2) loss of the α-H to the solvent forms the C=C and the O–H.
B⁻, −BH⟶ BH, −B⁻⟶
Base-catalysed enolisation: enolate intermediate

Keto form is usually more stable for simple aldehydes and ketones, because the C=O bond (≈ 745 kJ mol⁻¹) plus a C–H bond is stronger than the C=C plus O–H: the enol content of acetone and of cyclohexanone is far below 0.01 % (of the order of 10⁻⁶ % for acetone). The enol content rises dramatically when the enol is specially stabilised.

Factors that raise the enol content
FactorWhyExample (approximate enol content)
Aromatic enolthe enol is an aromatic ringphenol (≈ 100 % 'enol'; the keto form cyclohexa-2,4-dienone is not detectable)
Conjugation of the C=C of the enol with another C=O or π-bondextra delocalisationacetylacetone, 1,3-diketones, ethyl acetoacetate
Intramolecular hydrogen bond (six-membered chelate)the enol O–H···O=C ring stabilises it, in non-polar solventsacetylacetone (≈ 80 % neat; > 90 % in non-polar solvents; much lower in water)
Two carbonyls in the cyclic 1,3-relationship held in the correct geometrycyclohexane-1,3-dione, dimedone: enol is the major form in solution
Non-polar solventthe chelate is not disrupted by solventacetylacetone in hexane ≫ in water
Strained or crowded ketonesrelief of strain (rarely)
phenol (enol is aromatic) cyclohexa-2,4-dienone (keto) acetylacetone, keto acetylacetone, cis-enol ethyl acetoacetate, keto ethyl acetoacetate, enol
Tautomer pairs
IMP Acetylacetone and ethyl acetoacetate: the 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds have an unusually acidic CH₂ (pKₐ 9 and 11) and a strongly stabilised enol (the C=C is conjugated with the second C=O and the OH···O=C chelate ring). Acetylacetone is about 80 % enol in the pure liquid; ethyl acetoacetate about 8 % (ester C=O is a poorer acceptor and a poorer H-bond acceptor than ketone C=O). Both give a violet/red colour with FeCl₃ (enol/phenol test), decolourise bromine water (enol C=C), and react with sodium, but also give oxime/2,4-DNP derivatives (keto C=O): both forms are present.
Exam Trap Not every carbonyl can enolise. Enolisation needs a hydrogen on an sp³ α-carbon. HCHO, PhCHO, Ph₂CO, (CH₃)₃C–CHO and HCOOH have no α-H. Also, an α-H at a bridgehead of a small bicyclic ketone cannot enolise: the enol would put a double bond at the bridgehead (anti-Bredt).
Illustration 17.1 Main

Can it enolise?

Which of the following can exhibit keto–enol tautomerism: acetaldehyde, benzaldehyde, acetone, benzophenone, 2,2-dimethylpropanal, cyclohexanone, formaldehyde?

  1. A carbonyl compound enolises if it has at least one α-H.
  2. Yes: acetaldehyde (CH₃), acetone (CH₃), cyclohexanone (ring CH₂). No α-H: benzaldehyde, benzophenone, (CH₃)₃CCHO (α-carbon is quaternary), formaldehyde.
  3. Three of the seven.
Illustration 17.2 Main

Draw the enol forms

How many enol forms (constitutional) can butan-2-one (CH₃COCH₂CH₃) give? Also count the geometrical isomers.

  1. The α-carbons are C-1 (CH₃) and C-3 (CH₂): two constitutional enols.
  2. The C-3 enol, CH₃–CH=C(OH)–CH₃, has two different substituents on each double-bond carbon and exists as E and Z isomers; the C-1 enol, CH₂=C(OH)CH₂CH₃, does not.
  3. Total: 2 constitutional (3 counting E and Z separately).
butan-2-one enol toward C1 enol toward C3 (E/Z)
Illustration 17.3 Adv

Order of enol content

Arrange in increasing enol content: acetone, ethyl acetoacetate, acetylacetone, cyclohexanone.

  1. Simple ketones (acetone, cyclohexanone) have negligible enol; ethyl acetoacetate has about 8 %; acetylacetone about 80 %.
  2. acetone ≈ cyclohexanone (negligible) < ethyl acetoacetate < acetylacetone.
Illustration 17.4 Adv

Solvent effect on enol content

Acetylacetone is about 92 % enol in hexane and only about 15 % enol in water. Explain.

  1. In hexane the enol is stabilised by an intramolecular O–H···O hydrogen bond (chelate), which is the dominant intramolecular interaction in a non-polar medium. The enol's dipole moment is also smaller (the two C=O/C–O dipoles partly cancel in the chelate).
  2. In water the keto form (more polar, with two C=O groups free) is solvated by hydrogen bonds to water, and the enol's internal H-bond competes with H-bonds to the solvent; the equilibrium shifts toward the keto form.

HYF How to find the tautomers of any compound: look for the pattern H–X–Y=Z (X, Z = C, N, O, S) and write the isomer X=Y–Z–H. The H moves from the atom X to the atom Z; the double bond moves from Y=Z to X=Y. If X has no hydrogen (or Z is not electronegative enough to bear it) no tautomerism. For the keto form H–C–C=O: X = C(α), Y = C, Z = O.
Illustration 17.5 Main

Identify the tautomerism

Name the type of tautomerism: (a) CH₃CH=NCH₃ ⇌ CH₂=CH–NHCH₃ (b) CH₃CONH₂ ⇌ CH₃C(OH)=NH (c) CH₃NO₂ ⇌ CH₂=N(O)OH (d) CH₃CH=NOH ⇌ CH₃CH₂N=O.

  1. (a) imine–enamine. (b) amide–imidic acid (lactam–lactim type). (c) nitro–aci-nitro. (d) oxime–nitroso.
Illustration 17.6 Adv

Tautomers of a heterocycle

Draw the two tautomers of 2-hydroxypyridine and say which predominates in water.

  1. The H moves between oxygen and ring nitrogen. 2-Pyridone retains a six-π-electron aromatic ring (the N lone pair is in the sextet and C=O is polarised: pyridinium-olate resonance) and has strong intermolecular H-bonding and a larger dipole moment, so it predominates in water and in the solid.
  2. In the gas phase and in non-polar solvents the two forms are of comparable energy and the hydroxy form is slightly favoured.
2-hydroxypyridine (lactim) 2-pyridone (lactam)
Illustration 17.7 Adv

Racemisation and H–D exchange via enolisation

Why does optically active (R)-3-methylpentan-2-one racemise in aqueous base or acid and exchange its α-hydrogens with D in D₂O?

  1. The α-carbon (C-3) is the stereocentre and carries an H. Enolisation removes this H and makes C-3 sp² (planar) in the enol or enolate: the stereo-information is lost. Reprotonation can occur from either face, giving a racemic mixture.
  2. In D₂O the enolate is protonated by D⁺ (deuterium): after repeated enolisation all α-H (C-1 and C-3) are replaced by D.
(R)-3-methylpentan-2-one enol (planar, achiral)

Illustration 17.8 Adv

Distinguish

How would you distinguish acetone from acetylacetone using a single reagent? Explain the result.

  1. Add neutral FeCl₃ solution: acetylacetone gives an intense red/violet colour (the enol chelates Fe³⁺); acetone gives no colour change because its enol content is negligible.
  2. Alternative: Br₂/CCl₄ is decolourised immediately by acetylacetone (rapid reaction with the enol), whereas acetone reacts only slowly through the acid- or base-catalysed enolisation.

18. Hydrogen bonding and the physical properties of organic compounds

18.1 The hydrogen bond

A hydrogen bond is an attractive interaction X–H···Y between a hydrogen atom covalently bonded to a strongly electronegative atom X (F, O, N) and a lone pair on another electronegative atom Y (F, O, N; weaker with Cl, S, and π-systems). It is mostly electrostatic: the small, nearly bare proton is attracted to the lone pair.

  • Strength: 10–40 kJ mol⁻¹, about one-tenth of a covalent bond but ten times larger than van der Waals attractions. Order of strength: F–H···F (≈ 29) > O–H···O (≈ 21) > N–H···N (≈ 13) in typical values; the bond is strongest when X–H···Y is linear.
  • Intermolecular hydrogen bonds link separate molecules (association): raises boiling point, melting point, viscosity, solubility in water. Intramolecular hydrogen bonds close a ring inside one molecule (chelation): lowers boiling point, raises volatility, lowers solubility in water.
ethanol (O–H···O) acetic acid dimer (two O–H···O) water o-nitrophenol (intramolecular) p-nitrophenol (intermolecular)
Hydrogen-bonding molecules

Within a group the boiling point rises with molar mass (London forces), except that the hydrides of N, O and F are far higher than the trend because of hydrogen bonding; CH₄ is normal (C is not electronegative enough).

Rules, in order of importance for similar molar masses: (1) hydrogen bonding, (2) dipole–dipole interaction, (3) molecular size (London dispersion forces increase with surface area and number of electrons), (4) branching (compact molecules have lower b.p.).

Illustration 18.1 Main

Order of boiling points

Arrange in increasing boiling point: ethanol, dimethyl ether, propane, acetic acid.

  1. Propane (M = 44) has only London forces: −42 °C. Dimethyl ether (46) has a dipole but no H-bond donor: −24 °C. Ethanol has O–H···O: 78 °C. Acetic acid forms strongly hydrogen-bonded dimers and is more polar: 118 °C.
  2. propane < dimethyl ether < ethanol < acetic acid.
Illustration 18.2 Main

Isomeric amines

Arrange in decreasing boiling point: n-propylamine, ethylmethylamine, trimethylamine.

  1. All three are C₃H₉N, so the molar mass is the same. The number of N–H bonds capable of H-bonding: primary (2 N–H) > secondary (1 N–H) > tertiary (none).
  2. n-propylamine (48 °C) > ethylmethylamine (37 °C) > trimethylamine (3 °C).
Illustration 18.3 Adv

Why is the boiling point of an alkane lower with branching?

Explain the b.p. order n-pentane (36 °C) > isopentane (28 °C) > neopentane (9.5 °C).

  1. The three molecules have the same molar mass and the same type of interaction (London dispersion). London forces depend on the contact surface between molecules: a long chain has a large surface; a spherical molecule has the smallest area of contact.
  2. Branching reduces the surface area, so the intermolecular attraction falls and the boiling point decreases: linear > monobranched > dibranched (spherical).
n-pentane isopentane neopentane
Illustration 18.4 Adv

Why does a primary alcohol boil higher than a tertiary isomer?

Explain the b.p. order butan-1-ol (118 °C) > butan-2-ol (99.5 °C) > 2-methylpropan-2-ol (82 °C).

  1. The same O–H···O hydrogen bonding is present in each, so the difference arises from molecular shape. The primary alcohol is an extended chain with a large surface area for dispersion forces; the tertiary alcohol is nearly spherical (smaller surface) and its OH group is shielded by three methyl groups, which hinders hydrogen bonding.
butan-1-ol butan-2-ol tert-butyl alcohol

18.3 Melting points and crystal packing

The melting point depends on the strength of the intermolecular forces and on how well the molecules pack in the crystal lattice. Symmetric molecules pack well and therefore melt at a higher temperature than less symmetrical isomers of similar boiling point.

IMP Rules. (1) para isomers of disubstituted benzenes usually have the highest m.p. (the most symmetrical, best packed); meta is often the lowest. (2) trans isomers have higher m.p. than cis (more symmetrical, pack better) but lower dipole moment and usually lower b.p. than the cis isomer (cis-2-butene 3.7 °C vs trans 0.9 °C; cis-1,2-dichloroethene 60 °C vs trans 48 °C). (3) An intramolecular H-bond (ortho-nitrophenol, salicylaldehyde) gives a lower m.p. than the para isomer, whose H-bonds link the molecules. (4) The m.p. of even-carbon members of a homologous series is above the trend line (alternation): n-alkanes and dicarboxylic acids (oxalic 189, malonic 135, succinic 188, glutaric 98, adipic 153 °C): the even-carbon molecules pack better because their terminal groups lie on opposite sides.
Illustration 18.5 Main

Melting points of the isomers of dichlorobenzene

The m.p. of o-, m-, p-dichlorobenzene are −17, −25 and 53 °C. Explain the high m.p. of the para isomer even though it has the lowest dipole moment.

  1. The melting point depends on the crystal packing as well as on the intermolecular forces. The para isomer is the most symmetrical (a centre of symmetry): it packs into the crystal lattice most efficiently, so more energy is needed to break the lattice.
  2. The ortho and meta isomers are less symmetrical and pack poorly: lower m.p. (the dipole moment affects the boiling point more than the melting point).
Illustration 18.6 Adv

Maleic acid and fumaric acid

Maleic acid melts at 135 °C and fumaric acid at about 287 °C (sealed tube); maleic acid is far more soluble in water. Explain both facts.

  1. Fumaric acid (trans) is symmetrical (centrosymmetric) and its COOH groups are far apart, so each molecule forms intermolecular hydrogen bonds with neighbours in a tight, well-packed lattice: high m.p., low solubility.
  2. In maleic acid (cis) the two COOH groups are close and form an intramolecular hydrogen bond (in the monoanion; partly in the diacid), so it forms fewer intermolecular H-bonds. It is also more polar (dipole moment). It is therefore lower melting and more soluble in water.

18.4 Solubility

Like dissolves like. Polar and hydrogen-bonding compounds dissolve in polar solvents (water); non-polar compounds dissolve in non-polar solvents (hexane, benzene).

  • Alcohols: methanol, ethanol and propanols are miscible with water; butanol 7.7 g in 100 mL; pentanol about 2.2 g in 100 mL. As the non-polar alkyl chain grows, solubility drops. Branching raises solubility (t-butyl alcohol is miscible; n-butanol is not).
  • Carboxylic acids up to C₄ are miscible with water; from C₅ upward the solubility drops; benzoic acid is slightly soluble in cold water. Amines up to C₅ are soluble (H-bonds with water); aniline is slightly soluble (3.6 g in 100 mL).
  • Ethers are slightly soluble: diethyl ether about 7 g in 100 mL (the oxygen accepts H-bonds from water but cannot donate); THF and dioxane are miscible.
  • Ionic compounds and salts of organic acids/bases dissolve in water: RCOONa, RNH₃⁺Cl⁻ (the basis of extraction of acids with NaOH or NaHCO₃ and of amines with HCl).
  • Intramolecular H-bonding lowers solubility in water (o-nitrophenol is sparingly soluble, p-nitrophenol more soluble); intermolecular H-bonding with water raises it.

18.5 Carboxylic acid dimers and colligative properties

In the vapour phase and in non-polar solvents (benzene, CCl₄) carboxylic acids exist mainly as cyclic dimers held by two O–H···O hydrogen bonds. This explains the abnormally high boiling points (acetic acid 118 °C, b.p. > ethanol 78 °C), and the molar mass measured by freezing-point depression in benzene being twice the formula mass (for benzoic acid ≈ 244 g mol⁻¹ instead of 122; van't Hoff factor i = 0.5 for complete dimerisation). In water the acids hydrogen-bond to the solvent and are monomeric (or ionised).

Illustration 18.7 Adv

Molar mass of benzoic acid in benzene

A solution of 1.22 g of benzoic acid (formula mass 122) in 100 g of benzene lowers the freezing point by 0.28 K (K_f of benzene = 5.12 K kg mol⁻¹). Calculate the apparent molar mass and the degree of association to dimers.

  1. M(apparent) = K_f × w × 1000 / (ΔT_f × W) = 5.12 × 1.22 × 1000 / (0.28 × 100) = 223 g mol⁻¹ (about twice 122: the acid is dimerised).
  2. For 2A ⇌ A₂ with degree of association α, the number of particles per mole of acid is 1 − α/2, so i = 122/223 = 0.547.
  3. α = 2(1 − 0.547) = 0.91: about 91 % of the benzoic acid is present as dimers.

18.6 Water, ice and other consequences

  • Ice is less dense than water (0.917 vs 1.000 g cm⁻³ at 0 °C): in ice each oxygen is bonded to four H atoms (two covalent, two H-bonds) in an open tetrahedral cage; on melting some H-bonds break and the molecules fall into the holes. Water is densest at 4 °C.
  • H-bonding in biomolecules: the α-helix and β-sheet of proteins (C=O···H–N); the DNA double helix (A–T with two, G–C with three hydrogen bonds); cellulose.
  • High viscosity of glycerol, glycols, sulfuric acid.
  • Anomalously high heats of vaporisation of water, ammonia, HF.
Illustration 18.8 Main

Intra- vs intermolecular H-bonding

Match the property with the type of hydrogen bonding: (a) o-nitrophenol is steam volatile; (b) ethanol has a higher boiling point than dimethyl ether; (c) p-nitrophenol is not steam volatile; (d) salicylaldehyde has a lower boiling point than its para isomer.

  1. (a) intramolecular, (b) intermolecular, (c) intermolecular, (d) intramolecular in salicylaldehyde.
Illustration 18.9 Adv

Explain the ordering of melting points and boiling points of nitrophenols

o-Nitrophenol m.p. 45 °C, m-nitrophenol 97 °C, p-nitrophenol 114 °C. Which is steam volatile?

  1. In the ortho isomer the OH and NO₂ are close, so one intramolecular hydrogen bond forms and no intermolecular association occurs; the molecules are held only by weaker forces: low m.p. and volatile in steam.
  2. In the meta and para isomers the OH can only bond to a different molecule; the para isomer is the more symmetrical and packs best (highest m.p.).
  3. o-Nitrophenol only is steam volatile; this is the basis of its separation from the para isomer in nitration of phenol.
Illustration 18.10 Main

Boiling point order for hydrogen halides

Why is HF the only hydrogen halide with an abnormally high boiling point?

  1. Fluorine is the most electronegative element and F is small, so the H–F bond is highly polar and the strong F–H···F hydrogen bonds link HF molecules into zigzag chains (and cyclic hexamers in the vapour). HCl, HBr and HI hardly form H-bonds; their b.p. rises with molar mass: HCl −85, HBr −67, HI −35 °C. HF boils at +20 °C.

Summary sheet: physical properties

IMP (1) H-bonding raises b.p., m.p., solubility in water, viscosity. (2) Intramolecular H-bond: lowers b.p./m.p., makes the compound steam-volatile and less soluble in water. (3) Branching: lower b.p., higher m.p. when symmetrical. (4) cis: higher b.p. and higher dipole moment; trans: higher m.p. (5) p-isomer highest m.p. (6) Even-carbon members have higher m.p. than the odd neighbours. (7) Carboxylic acids dimerise in non-polar solvents. (8) Amides > acids > alcohols > amines > ketones > ethers > alkanes in b.p. for similar masses.

19. Electrophiles, nucleophiles, leaving groups and reaction types

19.1 Electrophiles and nucleophiles

  • An electrophile (E⁺, 'electron-loving') is a species that accepts an electron pair to form a new bond: it is positively charged or has an electron-deficient (δ⁺) atom or an empty orbital. It is a Lewis acid.
  • A nucleophile (Nu⁻, 'nucleus-loving') is a species that donates an electron pair to form a new bond: it carries a lone pair or a π-bond (or is negatively charged). It is a Lewis base.
  • A base attacks a hydrogen (H⁺); a nucleophile attacks a carbon (or another atom other than H). Same species, different role: basicity is a thermodynamic property (equilibrium with H⁺), nucleophilicity is kinetic (rate of attack on carbon).
Common electrophiles
ClassExamplesWhere met
CationicH⁺, H₃O⁺, NO₂⁺, NO⁺, Br⁺ (from Br₂/FeBr₃), R⁺, RCO⁺ (acylium), N₂⁺ (ArN₂⁺), Hg²⁺EAS, alkene addition, diazonium coupling
Neutral, electron-deficientBF₃, AlCl₃, FeBr₃, SO₃, :CCl₂ (carbene), R₃B, ZnCl₂Friedel–Crafts, Lewis acid catalysis, Reimer–Tiemann
Neutral with a polarised multiple bondC=O of aldehyde, ketone, ester, acid chloride; C≡N; CO₂; C=N⁺nucleophilic addition / acyl substitution
Polarised σ-bondCH₃–Br, R–X, epoxides, R–OTs, CH₃–ISN2, SN1
α,β-Unsaturated carbonyl (β-carbon)CH₂=CH–CHO, CH₂=CH–COCH₃Michael addition

Illustration 19.1 Main

Classify

Classify as electrophile (E) or nucleophile (Nu): NO₂⁺, CN⁻, BF₃, NH₃, AlCl₃, CH₃OH, :CCl₂, H₂O, CH₃⁺, R–MgBr, CH₃COCl, SO₃, C₆H₆.

  1. Electrophiles: NO₂⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, :CCl₂, CH₃⁺, CH₃COCl (the carbonyl carbon), SO₃.
  2. Nucleophiles: CN⁻, NH₃, CH₃OH, H₂O, R–MgBr (carbanion-like R), C₆H₆ (π-electrons, toward strong electrophiles).

19.2 Ambident nucleophiles

An ambident nucleophile has two nucleophilic sites. Which site reacts depends on the electrophile (hard/soft), the counter-ion and the solvent.

Ambident nucleophiles and their reactions
NucleophileSitesOutcome 1 (conditions)Outcome 2 (conditions)
CN⁻C, NKCN (ionic, SN2): alkyl nitriles R–C≡N (attack by C)AgCN (covalent, C bound to Ag): isocyanides R–N≡C (attack by N)
NO₂⁻N, OAgNO₂ (covalent): nitroalkanes R–NO₂ (attack by N)KNO₂ or NaNO₂ (ionic): alkyl nitrites R–O–N=O as the main product (attack by O)
EnolateC, Oalkyl halides (soft electrophiles): C-alkylationsilyl chlorides, acyl chlorides (hard electrophiles): O-attack (silyl enol ether, enol ester)
PhenoxideO, C (ortho/para)alkyl halides, polar aprotic solvent: O-alkylation (Williamson ether)protic solvent (H-bonded O): some C-alkylation
SCN⁻S, Nalkyl halides (SN2): R–SCN, thiocyanate (S-attack)carbocations (SN1): R–NCS, isothiocyanate (N-attack)
+ AgCN⟶
Ethyl bromide with AgCN gives ethyl isocyanide (attack through N)
+ KCN⟶
With KCN the nitrile is formed (attack through C)
+ AgNO₂⟶
AgNO₂ gives the nitroalkane
+ KNO₂⟶
KNO₂ gives the alkyl nitrite
IMP Rule for ambident anions (Kornblum): the more ionic the salt (or the more SN1-like the reaction), the more the more electronegative (harder, more charged) atom reacts: O of nitrite, N of cyanide in the case of Ag⁺-assisted ionisation. The more covalent the salt and the more SN2-like the reaction, the more the less electronegative, softer atom reacts: N of nitrite (with Ag), C of cyanide (with K⁺).

19.3 What makes a good nucleophile

Factors in nucleophilicity
FactorEffectExample
Chargeanion > neutral partnerOH⁻ ≫ H₂O; RO⁻ ≫ ROH; NH₂⁻ ≫ NH₃
Electronegativity (across a period)less electronegative = better donorR₃C⁻ > R₂N⁻ > RO⁻ > F⁻; NH₃ > H₂O
Size/polarisability (down a group) in protic solventslarger = better (anions less strongly solvated, more polarisable)I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻; RS⁻ > RO⁻; PH₃ > NH₃
Solventpolar protic (H₂O, ROH) solvates small anions by H-bonds and lowers their nucleophilicity; polar aprotic (DMSO, DMF, acetone, CH₃CN) leaves them 'naked'in DMSO: F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻ (reverse order)
Steric hindrancebulky = poor nucleophile (but still a strong base)(CH₃)₃CO⁻ is a strong base but poor nucleophile
Resonancedelocalised anion = weaker nucleophileRCOO⁻ ≪ RO⁻; the order of basicity is the same
α-effectan adjacent lone-pair atom raises nucleophilicityNH₂NH₂, HOO⁻, NH₂OH
Exam Trap Basicity and nucleophilicity usually move together but not always. In a protic solvent the order of nucleophilicity of halides is I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ (opposite to the order of basicity F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻), because small F⁻ is tightly solvated. Bulky bases (t-BuOK, LDA, DBU, DIPEA) are strong bases but weak nucleophiles.
Illustration 19.2 Main

Order of nucleophilicity

Arrange in decreasing nucleophilicity in methanol: I⁻, Br⁻, Cl⁻, F⁻.

  1. Methanol is a polar protic solvent: it hydrogen-bonds to small anions. F⁻ is the smallest and most strongly solvated (hindered); I⁻ is large, very polarisable and weakly solvated.
  2. I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻. In DMSO (aprotic) the order reverses to F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻ (the order of basicity).
Illustration 19.3 Main

Nucleophile vs base

Arrange in decreasing nucleophilicity (in water): CH₃S⁻, CH₃O⁻, CH₃COO⁻, H₂O.

  1. RS⁻ is more polarisable than RO⁻ (and in protic solvents sulfur is less strongly solvated). RO⁻ is a stronger nucleophile than the delocalised RCOO⁻; neutral water is the weakest.
  2. CH₃S⁻ > CH₃O⁻ > CH₃COO⁻ > H₂O.
Illustration 19.4 Adv

Same attacking atom: which is the better nucleophile?

(a) NH₃ or H₂O? (b) PH₃ or NH₃? (c) (CH₃)₃N or (C₂H₅)₃N toward CH₃I? (d) CH₃O⁻ or (CH₃)₃CO⁻ toward CH₃I?

  1. (a) NH₃ (N is less electronegative, holds its lone pair less tightly). (b) PH₃ (larger, more polarisable P; the lone pair is more readily distorted). (c) (CH₃)₃N: the three ethyl groups hinder approach of the larger electrophile; for small electrophiles like H⁺ the order of basicity is different. (d) CH₃O⁻: the bulky tert-butoxide attacks the carbon slowly but removes H⁺ easily (good base, poor nucleophile) — which is why t-BuOK is used for E2 elimination.

19.4 Leaving groups

In substitution and elimination reactions the group that departs, taking the bonding pair with it, is the leaving group. A good leaving group is a weak base (the conjugate base of a strong acid), stable as an anion or a neutral molecule, and polarisable.

Leaving group ability and the pKₐ of the conjugate acid
Leaving groupConjugate acidpKₐ of conjugate acidComment
CF₃SO₃⁻ (triflate)CF₃SO₃H−14extremely good
I⁻HI−10best halide
Br⁻HBr−9
Cl⁻HCl−7
p-CH₃C₆H₄SO₃⁻ (tosylate), CH₃SO₃⁻ (mesylate)TsOH, MsOH−2.8, −1.9excellent: made from alcohols and TsCl
H₂O (from ROH₂⁺)H₃O⁺−1.7good only after protonation
F⁻HF3.2poor in SN2 (C–F bond is very strong)
CH₃COO⁻CH₃COOH4.76moderate
HO⁻, RO⁻H₂O, ROH15.7, 16–18poor: need protonation (acid) to make ROH₂⁺
NH₂⁻, R⁻, H⁻NH₃, RH, H₂38, 50, 35essentially never leave in simple SN reactions (hydride can leave in Cannizzaro, E1cB, aldol retro)
IMP Leaving-group order for alkyl halides: R–I > R–Br > R–Cl ≫ R–F. This is opposite to the order of C–X bond polarity and follows the C–X bond strength (C–F 485, C–Cl 339, C–Br 285, C–I 213 kJ mol⁻¹) and the pKₐ of HX. Sulfonates (OTs, OMs) rank above halides; to make a good leaving group from an alcohol either protonate it (HX, H₂SO₄) or convert it to a sulfonate or alkyl halide (SOCl₂, PBr₃).
Illustration 19.5 Main

Rank the leaving groups

Arrange in decreasing leaving-group ability: Cl⁻, OH⁻, I⁻, CH₃COO⁻, F⁻, Br⁻.

  1. The weaker the base, the better the leaving group; use the pKₐ of the conjugate acid: HI (−10), HBr (−9), HCl (−7), HF (3.2), CH₃COOH (4.76), H₂O (15.7).
  2. I⁻ > Br⁻ > Cl⁻ > F⁻ > CH₃COO⁻ > OH⁻.
Illustration 19.6 Adv

Why does an alcohol need acid?

Explain why CH₃CH₂OH reacts with HBr but not with NaBr alone, and why NaBr/H₂SO₄ works.

  1. OH⁻ is a strong base and so a very poor leaving group: Br⁻ cannot displace it. In acid the O is protonated; H₂O is a good, neutral leaving group and Br⁻ attacks the carbon (SN2 for primary alcohols).
  2. NaBr + H₂SO₄ generates HBr in situ (and the acid medium protonates the alcohol), so the reaction proceeds.
+ +H⁺⟶ Br⁻, −H₂O⟶
Protonation makes water the leaving group (pKₐ of H₃O⁺ −1.7) instead of OH⁻ (pKₐ of H₂O 15.7)

19.5 Types of reactions

Reaction types and the properties that decide them
TypeDescriptionDecided by
Substitution (SN1, SN2, SNAr, SNi)one group replaced by anotherleaving group, nucleophile, substrate, solvent
Addition (electrophilic, nucleophilic, radical, concerted)π-bond converted to two σ-bondsstability of the intermediate (Markovnikov), electron demand
Elimination (E1, E2, E1cB)loss of two groups from adjacent atoms to form a π-bondbase strength, leaving group, β-H acidity, stability of alkene (Zaitsev)
Rearrangementmigration of an atom or groupstability of the new intermediate
Oxidation / reductionchange in oxidation statereagent
Condensationcombination with loss of a small molecule (H₂O)carbonyl reactivity and enolisation
Pericyclicconcerted cyclic reorganisation (Diels–Alder, Cope)orbital symmetry
IMP Hammond postulate. A transition state resembles the species (reactants, intermediate or products) closest to it in energy. For a highly exothermic step the TS is early and resembles the reactants (low selectivity: chlorination); for an endothermic step the TS is late and resembles the intermediate (high selectivity: bromination; stability of the carbocation or radical directly controls the rate). A more stable intermediate forms faster.
Illustration 19.7 Adv

Kinetic vs thermodynamic control

Addition of HBr to 1,3-butadiene gives at −80 °C mainly 3-bromobut-1-ene (1,2-adduct) and at +40 °C mainly 1-bromobut-2-ene (1,4-adduct). Explain using the allylic cation.

  1. H⁺ adds to C-1 to give the resonance-stabilised allylic cation (charge on C-2 and C-4). Br⁻ can attack either end.
  2. Low temperature (kinetic control): attack at C-2 (the carbon with the greater positive character, nearer the H–Br addition) is faster: 1,2-adduct. High temperature (thermodynamic control): the addition is reversible; the more stable (more substituted, internal) alkene — the 1,4-adduct — accumulates.
+ +H⁺⟶ ↔⟶
The allylic cation: positive charge shared between C-2 and C-4
3-bromobut-1-ene (1,2; kinetic) 1-bromobut-2-ene (1,4; thermodynamic)

Summary sheet: reagents

IMP (1) Electrophile = Lewis acid, attacks electron-rich sites; nucleophile = Lewis base, attacks δ⁺ carbon. (2) Basicity (H⁺ affinity) vs nucleophilicity (rate at carbon): I⁻ is a better nucleophile than F⁻ in water, a worse base; t-BuO⁻ is a good base, a poor nucleophile. (3) Ambident ions: KCN → RCN, AgCN → RNC; KNO₂ → RONO, AgNO₂ → RNO₂. (4) Leaving group ability follows the strength of the conjugate acid: TfO⁻, I⁻, Br⁻, TsO⁻, Cl⁻ ≫ F⁻ ≫ OH⁻, NH₂⁻. (5) Solvent: polar protic solvents favour SN1 and hinder small anions; polar aprotic solvents favour SN2.
