Detailed Solutions

A. Foundation

Solution 1
  1. m-nitrobenzoic acid (pKₐ 3.45): −I operates at meta (no direct resonance with the carboxylate carbon): strongly acid-strengthening.
  2. benzoic acid (pKₐ 4.20): reference.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, m-nitrobenzoic acid wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 2
  1. benzoic acid (pKₐ 4.20): reference.
  2. p-toluic acid (pKₐ 4.37): +I and hyperconjugation at para: acid-weakening.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, benzoic acid wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 3
  1. m-methoxybenzoic acid (pKₐ 4.09): only −I operates at meta: acid-strengthening.
  2. p-methoxybenzoic acid (pKₐ 4.47): +M outweighs −I at para: acid-weakening.
  3. Comparing the stability of the conjugate base: m-methoxybenzoic acid is the stronger acid — option B.
Solution 4
  1. o-chlorobenzoic acid (pKₐ 2.94): ortho effect (COOH twisted out of the ring plane: steric inhibition of resonance) together with the short-range effect of the substituent (−I (strong) and +M (weak)).
  2. p-chlorobenzoic acid (pKₐ 3.99): −I is opposed by +M at para: weaker effect than at meta.
  3. The stability of the conjugate base decides: o-chlorobenzoic acid is the stronger acid (option B).
Solution 5
  1. m-chlorobenzoic acid (pKₐ 3.83): only −I operates at meta: acid-strengthening.
  2. p-chlorobenzoic acid (pKₐ 3.99): −I is opposed by +M at para: weaker effect than at meta.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, m-chlorobenzoic acid wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 6
  1. o-toluic acid (pKₐ 3.91): ortho effect (COOH twisted out of the ring plane: steric inhibition of resonance) together with the short-range effect of the substituent (+I and hyperconjugation).
  2. p-toluic acid (pKₐ 4.37): +I and hyperconjugation at para: acid-weakening.
  3. The stability of the conjugate base decides: o-toluic acid is the stronger acid (option A).
Solution 7
  1. p-nitrobenzoic acid (pKₐ 3.44): −I plus −M at para: strongly acid-strengthening.
  2. p-toluic acid (pKₐ 4.37): +I and hyperconjugation at para: acid-weakening.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, p-nitrobenzoic acid wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 8
  1. p-nitrophenol (pKₐ 7.15): −M and −I: the phenoxide charge is delocalised onto NO₂.
  2. m-nitrophenol (pKₐ 8.39): only −I at meta (no resonance with the phenoxide oxygen).
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, p-nitrophenol wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 9
  1. phenol (pKₐ 9.99): reference.
  2. p-cresol (pKₐ 10.26): +I and hyperconjugation (destabilise the phenoxide).
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, phenol wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 10
  1. m-methoxyphenol (pKₐ 9.65): only −I at meta: acid-strengthening.
  2. p-methoxyphenol (pKₐ 10.21): +M outweighs −I at para: acid-weakening.
  3. Comparing the stability of the conjugate base: m-methoxyphenol is the stronger acid — option A.
Solution 11
  1. o-chlorophenol (pKₐ 8.56): −I strongest at ortho.
  2. p-chlorophenol (pKₐ 9.41): −I opposed by +M at para.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, o-chlorophenol wins as the stronger acid; answer A.
Solution 12
  1. p-cyanophenol (pKₐ 7.97): −M and −I at para.
  2. phenol (pKₐ 9.99): reference.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, p-cyanophenol wins as the stronger acid; answer A.
Solution 13
  1. formic acid (pKₐ 3.75): no alkyl group: reference for the +I effect.
  2. acetic acid (pKₐ 4.76): one +I methyl group.
  3. Comparing the stability of the conjugate base: formic acid is the stronger acid — option A.
Solution 14
  1. dichloroacetic acid (pKₐ 1.29): two α-Cl.
  2. chloroacetic acid (pKₐ 2.86): one α-Cl (−I).
  3. Comparing the stability of the conjugate base: dichloroacetic acid is the stronger acid — option B.
Solution 15
  1. trifluoroacetic acid (pKₐ 0.50): three α-F: strongest −I.
  2. trichloroacetic acid (pKₐ 0.70): three α-Cl: very strong −I.
  3. Comparing the stability of the conjugate base: trifluoroacetic acid is the stronger acid — option A.
Solution 16
  1. propiolic acid (pKₐ 1.84): sp α-carbon: strongest −I among the unsaturated acids.
  2. acrylic acid (pKₐ 4.25): sp² α-carbon: −I relative to sp³.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, propiolic acid wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 17
  1. 2-chlorobutanoic acid (pKₐ 2.84): Cl on the α-carbon.
  2. 4-chlorobutanoic acid (pKₐ 4.52): Cl on the γ-carbon: very weak effect.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, 2-chlorobutanoic acid wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 18
  1. methanol (pKₐ 15.50): smallest alkyl group, best solvated alkoxide.
  2. water (pKₐ 15.70): reference.
  3. Comparing the stability of the conjugate base: methanol is the stronger acid — option A.
Solution 19
  1. phenol (pKₐ 9.99): phenoxide is resonance-stabilised.
  2. 2,2,2-trifluoroethanol (pKₐ 12.40): −I of three F.
  3. On the stability of the conjugate base criterion, phenol wins as the stronger acid; answer B.
Solution 20
  1. methanethiol (pKₐ 10.30): S–H: larger atom, weaker bond.
  2. methanol (pKₐ 15.50): smallest alkyl group, best solvated alkoxide.
  3. The stability of the conjugate base decides: methanethiol is the stronger acid (option A).
Solution 21
  1. ethanol (pKₐ 15.90): +I of ethyl.
  2. tert-butyl alcohol (pKₐ 18): three +I methyls, hindered solvation of t-butoxide.
  3. Comparing the stability of the conjugate base: ethanol is the stronger acid — option B.
Solution 22
  1. ethyne (pKₐ 25): sp carbanion (50 % s).
  2. ethene (pKₐ 44): sp² carbanion (33 % s).
  3. The stability of the conjugate base decides: ethyne is the stronger acid (option B).
Solution 23
  1. cyclopentadiene (pKₐ 16): cyclopentadienide is aromatic (6π).
  2. cycloheptatriene (pKₐ 36): cycloheptatrienide would be anti-aromatic (8π).
  3. Comparing the stability of the conjugate base: cyclopentadiene is the stronger acid — option A.
Solution 24
  1. nitromethane (pKₐ 10.20): nitronate: delocalised onto two O atoms.
  2. acetone (pKₐ 19.30): enolate (C=O delocalisation).
  3. The stability of the conjugate base decides: nitromethane is the stronger acid (option A).
Solution 25
  1. acetylacetone (pKₐ 8.90): carbanion delocalised over two C=O.
  2. acetone (pKₐ 19.30): enolate (C=O delocalisation).
  3. The stability of the conjugate base decides: acetylacetone is the stronger acid (option A).
Solution 26
  1. triphenylmethane (pKₐ 30.60): charge over three phenyl rings.
  2. diphenylmethane (pKₐ 32.20): charge over two phenyl rings.
  3. The stability of the conjugate base decides: triphenylmethane is the stronger acid (option B).
Solution 27
  1. trichloroacetic acid (pKₐ 0.70): three α-Cl: very strong −I.
  2. chloroacetic acid (pKₐ 2.86): −I.
  3. acetic acid (pKₐ 4.76): reference (no substituent effect).
  4. trichloroacetic acid > chloroacetic acid > acetic acid — correct option D.
Solution 28

  1. benzene has μ = 0: D₆h symmetry.

  1. Formic acid pKₐ 3.75 < acetic acid 4.76: Statement I is true. The +I effect of CH₃ increases electron density on the carboxylate and destabilises it: Statement II is true and explains I: A.
Solution 552
  1. pKₐ 7.15 vs 8.39: I true. At para the O⁻ charge is delocalised onto NO₂ (−M) whereas at meta only the weaker −I effect acts: II true and explains I: A.
Solution 553
  1. Pyrrole (pKₐH −3.8) vs pyridine (5.2): I true. Protonation at N would remove the lone pair from the π-sextet and destroy aromaticity: II true and explains I: A.
Solution 554
  1. I is true: COT adopts a non-planar tub shape and behaves as a non-aromatic polyene. II is a true statement (8 = 4 × 2) but it is the reason for the *possibility* of anti-aromaticity, not for its absence: it does not explain I: B.
Solution 555
  1. 172 pm vs 177 pm: I true; II true and is the explanation (s-character and +M of Cl): A.
Solution 556
  1. In water t-BuOH (≈ 18) is weaker than MeOH (15.5): I true. In the gas phase the order reverses (t-BuOH is the stronger acid because polarisability of the alkyl groups stabilises the anion): II false: C.
Solution 557
  1. pKₐH: Me₂NH 10.73, Me₃N 9.80: I true. Me₃NH⁺ has one N–H and is less solvated (also more hindered): II true and explains I: A.

D. Advanced (JEE Advanced level)

Solution 558
  1. σ(p-OCH₃) = 4.20 − 4.47 = −0.27.
  2. A negative σ means the group is electron-donating from the para position: the +M effect of the methoxy oxygen outweighs its −I effect.
Solution 559
  1. pKₐ = 4.20 − 0.50 = 3.70.
  2. K_a ratio = 10^0.50 = 3.2 (the substituted acid is about three times stronger).
Solution 560
  1. At the meta position OCH₃ cannot conjugate with the carboxyl-bearing carbon, so only its −I effect (electronegative oxygen) acts: σ > 0. At para the +M effect donates and overrides −I: σ < 0.
  2. Cl is −I > +M. At meta only −I operates (0.37); at para +M partly cancels −I (0.21).
Solution 561
  1. Guanidine (13.6). The imino nitrogen is protonated; the guanidinium ion has three equivalent contributors with the charge shared over three nitrogens, giving the most stabilised conjugate acid.
guanidine
Solution 562
  1. K_b ∝ K_a(conjugate acid)^−1·K_w: ratio = 10^(11.12 − 5.23) = 10^5.89 ≈ 7.8 × 10⁵.
  2. Piperidine N is sp³ (25 % s), pyridine N is sp² (33 % s): the more s-character, the more tightly held the lone pair and the weaker the base. Pyridine's ring sp² carbons are also −I.
piperidine pyridine
Solution 563
  1. In water the stability of the conjugate acid depends on hydrogen bonding of N–H⁺ to solvent: Me₃NH⁺ has only one N–H and is hindered, Me₂NH₂⁺ has two. The loss of solvation outweighs the extra +I of the third methyl group.
  2. In the gas phase there is no solvent, so each added methyl group raises the proton affinity (NH₃ 854 < CH₃NH₂ 899 < (CH₃)₂NH 930 < (CH₃)₃N 949 kJ mol⁻¹).
Solution 564
  1. Cyclopentadiene gives the cyclopentadienyl anion, planar and cyclic with 6π electrons — aromatic. Cycloheptatriene would give the cycloheptatrienyl anion with 8π electrons — anti-aromatic and destabilised. K_a ratio = 10^(36 − 16) = 10²⁰.
cyclopentadiene cycloheptatriene
Solution 565
  1. K = 10^(15.7 − 16) = 10^(−0.3) = 0.50.
  2. Let x be the amount converted: x²/[(0.1 − x)²] = 0.50, so x/(0.1 − x) = 0.708, giving x = 0.0415 M: 41 % deprotonated. Hydroxide is only just strong enough; a stronger base (NaH, NaOEt in excess, NaNH₂) gives complete deprotonation.
Solution 566
  1. Cyclopentadiene (16) > indene (20) > fluorene (22.6) > toluene (41).
  2. Indene: deprotonation gives the indenyl anion, a cyclopentadienide ring fused to benzene (10π, aromatic); fusion with the benzene ring diverts some charge into the ring, so indene is a little less acidic than cyclopentadiene.
cyclopentadiene indene fluorene toluene
Solution 567
  1. The neopentyl cation, (CH₃)₃C–CH₂⁺, is primary. A methyl group migrates with its bonding electrons to the cationic carbon, giving (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₂CH₃ (tert-amyl cation), a tertiary cation.
1,2-CH₃ shift⟶
Solution 568
  1. tert-Amyl cation, (CH₃)₂C⁺–CH₂CH₃: two CH₃ (6 H) + one CH₂ (2 H) on the cationic carbon = 8 α-H. Neopentyl cation, CH₂⁺ attached to a quaternary carbon: 0 α-H.
  2. The shift converts a primary cation with no hyperconjugation into a tertiary one with eight α-H and three alkyl groups donating by +I: a large stabilisation, so the rearrangement is fast.
Solution 569
  1. The tert-amyl cation is trapped by water (substitution) to give 2-methylbutan-2-ol, or loses a β-proton (elimination, Zaitsev) to give the more substituted alkene 2-methylbut-2-ene.
  2. Neopentyl alcohol would require attack of water on the primary cation, which has already rearranged before it can be captured.
2-methylbutan-2-ol 2-methylbut-2-ene
Solution 570
  1. FeCl₃ colour (enol O–H, like phenol) and rapid bromine addition (C=C of the enol) → enol. 2,4-DNP condensation (ketone C=O) → keto.
  2. Both are observed because the two forms equilibrate quickly; as a reagent removes one, the equilibrium replenishes it.
keto form enol form
Solution 571
  1. The enol C=C is conjugated with the ester C=O, and the enol O–H forms a six-membered intramolecular hydrogen bond with the ester carbonyl oxygen (a chelate ring). These two features stabilise the enol relative to the keto form, whereas the enol of ethyl acetate or acetone has neither a conjugated C=O nor a chelate ring and is present only in traces.
Solution 572
  1. Hexane. In a non-polar solvent the intramolecular hydrogen bond is the dominant interaction and the enol is relatively less polar. In water the solvent H-bonds to the keto C=O groups and competes with the intramolecular bond: the keto form is favoured.
  2. Replacing OEt by CH₃ makes the second carbonyl a ketone (a better H-bond acceptor and a stronger −M acceptor than an ester, whose C=O is deactivated by O lone-pair donation), so the enol content rises to about 80 % in neat acetylacetone.
Solution 573
  1. o-Nitrophenol has an intramolecular O–H···O–N hydrogen bond (six-membered chelate ring); the molecules are not hydrogen-bonded to each other, so the vapour pressure is high and the compound is steam-volatile. In p-nitrophenol the OH and NO₂ are too far apart; the OH bonds to the NO₂ or OH of other molecules (association): high m.p., low volatility.
o-nitrophenol p-nitrophenol
Solution 574
  1. Ionisation of o-nitrophenol requires breaking the intramolecular hydrogen bond, which costs energy and offsets the larger −I effect of the adjacent NO₂ and the −M effect. The two acidities are therefore nearly equal (7.23 vs 7.15), with the para isomer very slightly stronger.
Solution 575
  1. p-Nitrophenol is more soluble in water: its OH and NO₂ groups are free to hydrogen-bond with water molecules. In the ortho isomer the OH is already tied up in the intramolecular bond and cannot bond to water: it is less soluble in water, more soluble in non-polar solvents.
Solution 576
  1. Para: the aniline vector (NH₂ → ring, along the axis toward NO₂) and the nitrobenzene vector (ring → NO₂) point the same way: μ = 4.0 + 1.5 = 5.5 D (measured 6.2 D).
  2. Meta: the substituents are 120° apart on the ring, but the NH₂ moment points toward the ring and the NO₂ moment points away from it, so the angle between the two moment vectors is 60°: μ² = 4.0² + 1.5² + 2(4.0)(1.5)cos 60° = 16 + 2.25 + 6.0 = 24.25, μ = 4.9 D (measured 4.9 D).
p-nitroaniline m-nitroaniline
Solution 577
  1. At para the donor NH₂ and the acceptor NO₂ are conjugated through the ring: the lone pair is delocalised onto the nitro oxygens (quinoid contribution), which adds extra charge separation and therefore an extra moment (6.2 − 5.5 = 0.7 D). At meta no such through-ring conjugation between the two groups is possible, so the moment is just the vector sum.
↔⟶
Solution 578
  1. The two ortho methyls twist the NMe₂ group out of the ring plane (steric inhibition of resonance): the push–pull conjugation is lost, so the dipole moment decreases toward the simple vector sum.
  2. The NMe₂ lone pair is no longer delocalised into the ring, so its basicity increases (it behaves like an aliphatic tertiary amine).
Solution 579
  1. Total stabilisation = 137 − 111 = 26 kJ mol⁻¹ for four methyl groups: ≈ 6.5 kJ mol⁻¹ per methyl on average (the first methyl contributes 11 kJ mol⁻¹, as shown by ethene → propene, later ones less).
Solution 580
  1. The number of α-hydrogens is not the only factor: in trans-2-butene the two methyl groups are on different carbons (1,2-disubstituted), in 2-methylpropene both are on the same carbon (1,1-disubstituted). Experimentally 1,2-disubstituted (trans) alkenes are slightly more stable than 1,1-disubstituted isomers, so trans-2-butene has the smaller heat of hydrogenation (116 vs 119 kJ mol⁻¹). Hyperconjugation counting alone cannot resolve such small differences.
trans-2-butene 2-methylpropene
Solution 581
  1. It is a trisubstituted alkene with three methyl groups on the double bond: 9 α-H. It is more stable than trans-2-butene (6 α-H), so its heat of hydrogenation is smaller in magnitude, about −113 kJ mol⁻¹, i.e. above −116 (less negative).
2-methyl-2-butene

  1. Propane has 6 primary H and 2 secondary H. Relative amounts: primary 6 × 1 = 6; secondary 2 × 3.8 = 7.6.
  2. Fraction of 2-chloropropane = 7.6/(6 + 7.6) = 0.559 = 56 %.
propane
Solution 583
  1. Secondary: 2 × 82 = 164; primary: 6 × 1 = 6. Fraction of 2-bromopropane = 164/170 = 96.5 %.
  2. Br• abstracts H in an endothermic step: the transition state is late and resembles the alkyl radical, so the stability difference between 2° and 1° radicals is fully expressed (high selectivity). Cl• abstraction is exothermic with an early transition state, so the radical stability matters less.

  1. Primary: 9 × 1 = 9; tertiary: 1 × 5 = 5. Tertiary fraction = 5/14 = 36 %.

Solution 585
  1. The N-methylpyrrolidine nitrogen (sp³, trialkylamine type, pKₐH 8.0) is far more basic than the pyridine nitrogen (sp², pKₐH 3.1, and with a −I substituent at C-3).
  2. The pyrrolidine N is protonated first.
nicotine
Solution 586
  1. The side-chain primary amine (conjugate acid pKₐ 9.8) is the stronger base. At pH 7.4 it is protonated (pH < 9.8) while the imidazole (pKₐ 6.0) is mostly neutral (pH > 6.0): the main species is the mono-cation with the NH₃⁺ side chain.
histamine
Solution 587
  1. The exocyclic NH₂ lone pair is conjugated with the ring; protonating it would break that conjugation. Protonation at the ring N gives a cation in which the NH₂ lone pair delocalises onto the ring nitrogen (amidinium-type resonance, N–C=C–C=N⁺ ↔ N⁺=C–C=C–N), a very stable ion.
  2. The +M effect of NH₂ at the para position raises the electron density on ring N and stabilises the cation: pKₐH 9.2 vs 5.2.

the cation: amidinium-like resonance between ring N–H and exocyclic NH₂

  1. Ortho: −I at the shortest distance, ortho effect, and the intramolecular O–H···⁻OOC hydrogen bond that stabilises the carboxylate: strongest. Meta: only −I operates: stronger than benzoic (4.20). Para: +M of OH outweighs −I: weaker than benzoic acid.

salicylic acid m-hydroxybenzoic acid p-hydroxybenzoic acid

  1. K = K_a(p-nitrophenol)/K_a(phenol) = 10^(9.99 − 7.15) = 10^2.84 = 6.9 × 10².

  1. pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 4.20 + log 10 = 5.20.

  1. The dipole of the first three arises only from the difference in s-character of the carbon atoms of the σ-bond (sp³–sp³ : none; sp³–sp²: 25 → 33 %; sp³–sp: 25 → 50 %) and the hyperconjugation toward the unsaturated carbon.

propane propene propyne acetonitrile
Solution 594
  1. Benzylamine 9.34 > N-methylaniline 4.85 > aniline 4.60 > p-nitroaniline 1.00 > acetamide −0.5.
  2. (iii) > (iv) > (i) > (ii) > (v). An sp³ N with a non-conjugated lone pair is the strongest; a lone pair conjugated to the ring is weaker (anilines), still weaker with a −M group, and weakest when it is conjugated with a carbonyl (amide).
Solution 595
  1. The carbanion is stabilised by delocalisation onto two C=O groups; a ketone C=O is a better acceptor than an ester C=O (in esters the OR lone pair donates into C=O and reduces its electron-withdrawing power). Two ketones (acetylacetone) > ketone + ester (acetoacetate) > two esters (malonate). With a single ketone group (acetone) the stabilisation is only half as effective: pKₐ 19.3, about 10 pKₐ units weaker than acetylacetone.
Solution 596
  1. (i) The trityl cation is delocalised over three phenyl rings (ortho and para carbons of each ring): it is so stable that its salts can be isolated. (ii) The t-butyl cation is stabilised by nine α-hydrogens (hyperconjugation) and three +I groups. (iii) The ethyl cation has only three α-hydrogens. (iv) The vinyl cation has an sp-hybridised cationic carbon: the empty p orbital is in the plane, not conjugated, and the carbon is more electronegative.
  2. (i) > (ii) > (iii) > (iv).
Solution 597
  1. Azulene has 10 π-electrons. In the dipolar resonance structure one electron moves from the seven-membered ring to the five-membered ring: the 5-ring becomes a 6π cyclopentadienide (δ⁻) and the 7-ring a 6π tropylium (δ⁺).
  2. Five-membered ring δ⁻; total 10π; 6π + 6π in the dipolar form (the two rings share the two electrons of the common C–C bond). Dipole moment = 1.0 D.
azulene

  1. Each has the exocyclic CH₂ structure (2 Kekulé) plus the three structures with the charge/electron at o, o, p ring carbons: 5 contributors each.
  2. The charge or odd electron is spread over 4 carbons (the CH₂ carbon and the o, o, p ring carbons).

  1. Carbons: two CH₃ on C-2 (sp³), C-2 (=C, sp²), the central allenic carbon (sp), CH= (sp²), two alkyne carbons (sp, sp), and the terminal CH₃ (sp³). Totals: sp³ = 3, sp² = 2, sp = 3.
  2. Bonds: C=C (1σ + 1π), C=C (1σ + 1π), C≡C (1σ + 2π), plus single bonds: C–C: C-2–CH₃ (2), CH–C≡ (1), ≡C–CH₃ (1) = 4 σ; C–H: 6 + 1 + 3 = 10 σ. Total σ = 3 + 4 + 10 = 17; π = 4.

Solution 600
  1. Acetone pKₐ 19.3. NaOH/NaOEt (conjugate acids 15.7, 15.9) lie below it: K = 10^(15.9 − 19.3) = 10^(−3.4): only about 0.04 % of acetone is converted at equilibrium (which is why the aldol reaction can proceed in equilibrium with a little enolate). NaNH₂ and LDA (conjugate acids 38, 36) are much stronger: K ≈ 10^16.7 (LDA) and 10^18.7 (NaNH₂): complete conversion, with LDA preferred because it is a bulky, non-nucleophilic base that does not add to the C=O.

  1. NaCN is ionic: the free cyanide ion attacks through carbon (the carbon lone pair is the more nucleophilic site in an SN2 reaction), giving R–C≡N.

  1. indole: aromatic; cyclopentadienyl anion: aromatic; cycloheptatrienyl anion: anti-aromatic; p-benzoquinone: non-aromatic; borole: anti-aromatic.
